Trouble disengaging from one task and fully engaging with another, which can create a lag or loss of momentum every time attention needs to move. This can make multitasking and interruptions especially costly for someone with ADHD.

Example: Pulled away from a spreadsheet to answer a coworker's quick question, a man loses ten minutes trying to remember what he was doing before the interruption.

See also: Cognitive Flexibility, Momentum And Activation

docs.title: Telehealth Evaluations
docs.text:
ADHD assessments and follow-up appointments conducted remotely by video rather than in person, which expanded significantly and became more accepted after 2020. Telehealth has improved access to evaluation for people in areas with few nearby specialists, though some jurisdictions place limits on prescribing controlled substances this way.

See also: Finding A Clinician, Controlled Substance Rules

docs.title: Telling A New Partner
docs.text:
The decision of when and how to disclose an ADHD diagnosis to a new romantic partner, which is a personal choice with no single correct timing. Framing the conversation around practical impact, such as how attention or memory show up day to day, tends to be more useful to a partner than the label alone.

Example: A woman waits until the third date to explain her ADHD, choosing a calm moment rather than blurting it out during an early awkward silence.

See also: ADHD And Dating, Disclosure To Friends

docs.title: Test-Taking Strategies
docs.text:
Approaches to exam performance that address ADHD-related challenges, such as reading all questions before starting, using extended time when available, and working through easier questions first to build momentum. These strategies aim to reduce the impact of time pressure and distractibility on demonstrating actual knowledge.

Example: A student reads through the entire exam once before answering anything, so a hard question early on doesn't eat up all her remaining time.

See also: School Accommodations, Momentum And Activation

docs.title: Tic Disorders
docs.text:
Conditions marked by sudden, repetitive, non-rhythmic movements or vocalizations, which occur more frequently in people with ADHD than in the general population. Because certain stimulant medications can occasionally worsen tics, prescribers weigh this history when choosing a treatment plan.

Example: A boy on a stimulant develops a new eye-blinking tic, prompting his parents and prescriber to discuss whether to adjust his medication.

See also: Comorbidity, Medication And Comorbidities

docs.title: Time Blindness
docs.text:
Difficulty sensing how much time has passed or how much remains, making it hard to estimate, track, or plan around time without external cues. Time blindness is a common and often misunderstood ADHD trait, frequently mistaken for not caring about being on time.

Example: Believing only twenty minutes have passed when in fact two hours have gone by.

See also: Time Estimation, Hyperfocus

docs.title: Time Estimation
docs.text:
The skill of accurately predicting how long a task will take to complete, which is frequently distorted in ADHD due to time blindness. Poor time estimation often leads to a cycle of underestimating how long tasks take and running chronically late as a result.

Example: A woman guesses a task will take twenty minutes and is surprised, again, when it takes two hours, so she starts doubling her estimates by habit.

See also: Time Blindness, Deadline Scaffolding

docs.title: Timers And Alarms
docs.text:
External tools used to mark the passage of time or signal when to start, stop, or switch a task, compensating for the internal difficulty many people with ADHD have sensing time. Timers work best when set for concrete, specific actions rather than vague reminders to "check in."

Example: A man sets a timer labeled "leave for the dentist" fifteen minutes before he actually needs to walk out the door, since a vague sense of time isn't enough.

See also: Time Blindness, Pomodoro Technique

docs.title: Titration
docs.text:
The gradual process of adjusting a medication's dose, usually starting low and increasing over time, to find the amount that provides the best symptom control with the fewest side effects. Titration is a normal part of starting ADHD medication and typically requires several follow-up appointments.

Example: A prescriber starts a patient on a low dose of medication and checks in every two weeks, nudging the amount up slightly until focus improves without troubling side effects.

See also: Finding The Right Dose, Side Effects

docs.title: To-Do Lists That Work
docs.text:
Task lists structured in a way that accounts for ADHD-related challenges, such as keeping the list short, specific, and visible, rather than long and abstract. A to-do list that works is usually reviewed at set times during the day, not left to be checked only when remembered.

Example: A man switches from one long, ever-growing list to a short list of just three items each morning, and finally starts finishing what's on it.

See also: Task Breakdown, Prioritization Methods

docs.title: Tracking Medication Response
docs.text:
The practice of monitoring how well an ADHD medication is working and what side effects appear, often using notes, apps, or rating scales shared with a prescriber. Tracking response over time gives a prescriber the information needed to fine-tune dose and timing.

Example: A man keeps a simple note on his phone each week rating his focus and mood, so his prescriber has real data instead of a vague "it's fine" at each visit.

See also: Finding The Right Dose, Measuring Treatment Progress

docs.title: Transition To College
docs.text:
The shift from a structured, closely supervised high school environment to the greater independence and looser oversight of college life. This transition is a common point at which previously compensated ADHD symptoms become disruptive enough to prompt an evaluation.

Example: A freshman who always had a parent checking his homework folder now has no one checking anything, and three assignments slip through the cracks in his first month.

See also: ADHD In College Years, College Disability Services

docs.title: Transition To Work
docs.text:
The shift from the academic structure of school into the different demands of a workplace, including new expectations around punctuality, self-direction, and long-term planning. Many adults first notice how much ADHD affects them during this transition, once external structure decreases.

Example: A new graduate who thrived with school deadlines and semesters finds the open-ended, self-directed pace of her first job far harder to structure on her own.

See also: ADHD In Adulthood, Career Fit

docs.title: Trauma And ADHD
docs.text:
The relationship between traumatic experiences and ADHD, which can occur together, resemble each other in some symptoms like difficulty concentrating, and even influence each other's severity. Careful evaluation is needed because trauma-related symptoms and ADHD symptoms can be mistaken for one another.

Example: A therapist works carefully to figure out whether a child's inability to concentrate in class comes from ADHD, from an unstable home situation, or from both at once.

See also: Chronic Stress Effects, Differential Diagnosis

docs.title: Treatment Evidence Hierarchy
docs.text:
A framework for ranking the strength of evidence behind a treatment, from large randomized controlled trials at the top down to individual testimonials at the bottom. Using this hierarchy helps separate well-supported ADHD treatments from those resting mainly on anecdote.

See also: Evidence-Based Information, Evaluating Treatment Claims

docs.title: Treatment Order Decisions
docs.text:
Clinical judgments about which condition to treat first when a person has ADHD along with a co-occurring condition, such as treating severe depression before starting ADHD medication. These decisions are made case by case, since the right order depends on which condition is causing the most immediate impairment.

See also: Integrated Treatment Planning, Comorbidity

docs.title: Underdiagnosis
docs.text:
The pattern of ADHD going unrecognized in groups where symptoms present differently than the stereotype clinicians were trained to spot, especially girls, women, and adults with strong compensation strategies. Underdiagnosis means many people live for years without access to support that could have helped them.

See also: Gender Diagnosis Gap, Masking

docs.title: Visual Reminders
docs.text:
Reminders placed where they can be seen repeatedly throughout the day, such as sticky notes or whiteboards, taking advantage of visible cues rather than relying on memory alone to prompt action. Visual reminders work especially well for tasks that are easy to forget simply because they are out of sight.

Example: A sticky note on the bathroom mirror reminds a teenager to pack her gym clothes, since a note buried in her phone would never get seen in time.

See also: Environment Design, Reminder Apps

docs.title: What A Diagnosis Means
docs.text:
The practical and personal significance of receiving an ADHD diagnosis: access to treatment and accommodations, a framework for understanding past struggles, and the start of building a more effective set of supports. A diagnosis describes a pattern of brain-based difference — it does not define a person's worth or potential.

See also: Reframing Your Past, Identity After Diagnosis

docs.title: When To Seek Help
docs.text:
The point at which ADHD-related struggles are significant or persistent enough to warrant a professional evaluation, generally when symptoms are causing real difficulty at school, work, or in relationships. There is no need to wait for a crisis — ongoing impairment is reason enough to seek an evaluation.

Example: A man finally books an evaluation after missing a third work deadline in a month, deciding the pattern is now too consistent to ignore.

See also: Diagnostic Evaluation, Finding A Clinician

docs.title: Who Can Diagnose ADHD
docs.text:
The range of licensed professionals qualified to evaluate and diagnose ADHD, including psychiatrists, psychologists, and some primary care providers, depending on training and local regulations. Knowing this range helps people find an appropriate clinician instead of assuming only one type of specialist can help.

See also: Psychiatrists, Psychologists

docs.title: Willpower Myth
docs.text:
The false belief that ADHD symptoms can be overcome simply by trying harder or wanting success badly enough. This myth ignores that ADHD involves measurable differences in brain chemistry and structure that willpower alone does not change.

Example: A father tells his son to "just focus harder" on his homework, not realizing the boy has already tried everything he knows how to try.

See also: Laziness Myth, ADHD As Regulation Difference

docs.title: Working Memory
docs.text:
The ability to hold information in mind and use it briefly while completing a task, such as remembering a set of instructions long enough to follow them. Weak working memory is one of the most consistent difficulties found in ADHD.

Example: Walking into a room to get something and forgetting what it was by the time you arrive.

See also: Executive Function, Prospective Memory

docs.title: Working With A Manager
docs.text:
The relationship between an employee with ADHD and their supervisor, which can be improved by clear, specific communication about how instructions, deadlines, and feedback are best delivered and received. A good working relationship with a manager often depends less on disclosure and more on establishing practical communication habits.

Example: An employee asks his manager to send follow-up instructions by email after every conversation, since he tends to lose details from spoken requests alone.

See also: Workplace Disclosure, Handling Feedback At Work

docs.title: Workplace Accommodations
docs.text:
Adjustments an employer provides to help an employee with ADHD perform their job effectively, such as written instructions, noise-reducing headphones, or flexible deadlines. In the U.S., workplace accommodations are generally requested and protected under the ADA.

Example: An employer agrees to give a woman written follow-ups after every verbal meeting, since she processes instructions on paper better than out loud.

See also: ADA Basics, Workplace Disclosure

docs.title: Workplace Disclosure
docs.text:
The personal decision of whether, when, and how much to tell an employer about an ADHD diagnosis, which is generally required only if formally requesting accommodations under the ADA. Disclosure is optional in most everyday situations and depends on what an individual judges will help versus create risk in their specific workplace.

Example: A man decides to tell only his direct manager about his ADHD, specifically to formally request noise-canceling headphones at his desk.

See also: ADA Basics, Self-Advocacy

docs.title: Writing With ADHD
docs.text:
The particular challenges ADHD can create around producing written work, including difficulty organizing ideas, starting a first draft, and staying on topic. Breaking writing into small, defined stages, such as outlining, drafting, and editing as separate steps, can make the process far more manageable.

Example: A student who freezes staring at a blank page finds it easier to first record a rough voice memo of her ideas, then turn that into an outline.

See also: Task Breakdown, Task Initiation

docs.title: Years Of Negative Feedback
docs.text:
The cumulative effect of receiving repeated criticism, correction, or discipline over childhood and adulthood because of ADHD symptoms that were not recognized or understood at the time. This accumulated feedback is a major, well-documented contributor to the anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem that often accompany ADHD.

Example: By the time she's thirty, a woman has heard some version of "if you'd just try harder" so many times from teachers and bosses that she's started to believe it herself.

See also: Shame And ADHD, Depression

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 15 chapters covering 300 concepts from the learning graph.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. What ADHD Is And Is Not - This chapter lays the foundation for everything that follows: what attention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity actually are, how ADHD is formally defined, and where it comes from.
  2. The ADHD Brain - This chapter explains how the ADHD brain works: brain development, executive function and its components, dopamine and the reward system, and why motivation behaves differently.
  3. Presentations And Everyday Traits - This chapter covers the three official presentations of ADHD and the everyday traits families actually recognize: hyperfocus, time blindness, procrastination, forgetfulness, and the inconsistency that confuses everyone.
  4. ADHD Across The Lifespan - This chapter follows ADHD from childhood through adulthood, with special attention to how it shows up in girls and women and why so many are diagnosed late.
  5. Getting A Diagnosis - This chapter walks through the diagnostic process end to end: who can diagnose, what an evaluation involves, how to prepare, and what the report does and does not mean.
  6. Co-occurring Conditions - This chapter covers the conditions that commonly travel with ADHD — anxiety, depression, learning disabilities, autism, sleep disorders — plus ADHD burnout.
  7. Medication - This chapter explains ADHD medication without hype or fear: how stimulants and non-stimulants work, what titration is, what side effects to watch, and how to track whether a medication is actually helping.
  8. Treatment Beyond Medication - This chapter surveys everything beyond medication with evidence behind it: behavioral therapy, CBT, ADHD coaching, exercise, sleep, nutrition, and mindfulness.
  9. Building Daily Systems - This chapter begins the practical toolkit: externalizing memory instead of trusting it, breaking tasks down, estimating time, using timers, body doubling, and building routines that fit an ADHD brain.
  10. Tools And Keeping Systems Alive - This chapter continues the toolkit with the physical and digital environment: visual reminders, decluttering, calendars, planners, distraction blockers, and prioritization.
  11. Emotional Life And Identity - This chapter addresses the emotional side of ADHD that rarely makes the diagnostic checklists: emotional dysregulation, rejection sensitivity, shame from years of negative feedback, and the grief and relief of a late diagnosis.
  12. School And College - This chapter covers learning with ADHD from study strategies through formal accommodations: IEPs and 504 plans in school, disability services in college, and how to actually request help.
  13. Work And Career - This chapter takes ADHD to work: finding career fit, workplace accommodations and the ADA, the disclosure decision, managing meetings and deadlines, and preventing burnout.
  14. Family Life And Communication - This chapter is where the book's two audiences meet: how ADHD lands on a family system, what the caregiver role really is, and how to support an adult family member without slipping into parenting them.
  15. Partners And Caring For The Caregiver - The final chapter covers romantic partnership with ADHD — dating, telling a new partner, the partner-parent trap, dividing the mental load — and then turns to the caregivers themselves: strain, burnout, boundaries, and support.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Chapters are ordered so that every concept appears after its prerequisites — reading in order always works. The book is also built for the two of you to read together: most chapters address the person with ADHD and their caregivers side by side, so reading the same chapter and comparing notes is a feature, not a shortcut.

Note: Each chapter lists the concepts it covers. Complete prerequisite chapters before moving to advanced ones.

docs.title: What ADHD Is And Is Not
Summary
docs.text: This chapter lays the foundation for everything that follows: what attention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity actually are, how ADHD is formally defined, and where it comes from. It also clears the ground of the myths — laziness, weak willpower, low intelligence — that make life harder for people with ADHD and their families. After this chapter, both readers share a common vocabulary and can tell evidence from misinformation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

Somebody in your life was just diagnosed with ADHD. Maybe it was you. Maybe it was your daughter, your husband, your sister, your roommate. Either way, you probably arrived here with a head full of half-remembered ideas about what ADHD is — a hyper kid bouncing off classroom walls, someone who "can't focus," a condition you're supposed to outgrow. Some of those ideas are partly right. Several are flat wrong, and the wrong ones do damage.

This chapter builds the vocabulary the rest of the book depends on. We'll define attention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity carefully, because those everyday words mean something more precise here. Then we'll assemble them into the formal definition of ADHD, look at where the condition comes from, and take apart the myths one at a time. If you and the person you care about each read this chapter and compare notes, you'll be having the first of many conversations this book is designed to start.

docs.title: Attention: More Than One Thing
docs.text:
Attention is the brain's ability to select some information for processing and set the rest aside. Right now, your brain is receiving far more input than it can use: the hum of a refrigerator, the pressure of the chair, a conversation in the next room, this sentence. Attention is the mechanism that picks this sentence and mutes the rest.

A useful way to picture it is a spotlight in a dark theater. The stage is full of actors, but the spotlight lights only one or two at a time. Everything else is still there — you just don't process it deeply. And the spotlight has an operator: something has to decide where the light points, how wide the beam is, how long it stays, and when it moves.

That operator matters more than the light. Attention is really a set of separate skills working together:

  • Selecting — choosing one target out of many (listening to one voice at a noisy dinner table)
  • Sustaining — holding on a target over time (reading a full chapter, finishing a form)
  • Resisting capture — keeping the beam from being yanked away by something louder, newer, or more interesting
  • Shifting — deliberately moving the beam when the task changes, then settling on the new target
  • Dividing — juggling two targets when you must (driving while following spoken directions)

Here's a worked example both readers will recognize. It's 8 pm and there's a form to fill out — insurance, school registration, it doesn't matter. Sitting down with the form requires selecting it over the phone lying next to it. Question 12 is confusing, and working through it requires sustaining attention through boredom and mild frustration. The phone buzzes; resisting capture means the buzz stays background noise. Halfway through, dinner needs stirring — shifting means going to the stove and then actually coming back to question 12, not discovering the form three hours later. A person whose spotlight operator works smoothly experiences this evening as unremarkable. A person with ADHD may fight a genuine battle at every one of those steps — and the form may still be unfinished at midnight, not because they didn't care, but because each step costs them far more than it appears to cost everyone else.

Before you try the simulation below, keep those five skills in mind — it puts you in the operator's seat so you can feel what each one costs.

docs.title: Diagram: Attention Spotlight Simulator
docs.text:
Run the Attention Spotlight Simulator fullscreen

Attention Spotlight Simulator

Type: microsim sim-id: attention-spotlight-simulator Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Learning objective: Understand (L2, Bloom verb: explain) that attention is a set of distinct skills — selecting, sustaining, resisting capture, and shifting — by operating a spotlight and experiencing each skill as a separate control problem.

Canvas layout: Responsive. Main drawing area (roughly 70% of width) shows a dim "stage" scattered with 8-10 labeled items (a form, a phone, a TV, a conversation bubble, a stove, a window, a clock). Right panel (roughly 30%) holds controls and a running score/infobox. On narrow screens the panel moves below the stage.

Visual elements:

  • A circular spotlight the learner drags with mouse or touch; items inside the beam brighten, items outside stay dim
  • A "task target" item outlined in green (the form) that the learner must keep lit
  • Distractor items that periodically pulse, grow, or flash (the phone buzzes, the TV flickers) and, if the spotlight drifts to them, capture the beam — the beam sticks to them for 2 seconds before it can be dragged away
  • A focus meter that fills while the target is lit and drains while it is not
  • A stage-2 mode where the target switches every 15 seconds (the stove needs stirring, then back to the form) to exercise shifting

Interactive controls:

  • Button: "Start" / "Reset"
  • Slider: Distraction intensity (how often and how strongly distractors pulse), default mid-range
  • Slider: Capture stickiness (how long a distractor holds the beam once it grabs it), default 2 seconds
  • Toggle: "Task switch mode" on/off, default off

Data visibility requirements:

  • Stage 1: Show the focus meter filling only while the beam is on the target
  • Stage 2: When a distractor captures the beam, show a caption naming what happened ("Capture: the phone buzz pulled the spotlight")
  • Stage 3: In task-switch mode, show elapsed time between the switch cue and the learner re-settling on the new target, labeled "shift cost"
  • Final: After 60 seconds, show a summary panel — time on target, number of captures, average shift cost — with one sentence connecting each number to the named attention skill

Behavior: Raising distraction intensity and capture stickiness models a higher-ADHD-load environment; the learner directly feels that the same task gets harder even though "trying" stays constant. The summary panel makes that explicit.

Instructional rationale: An Understand-level objective needs the learner to experience each sub-skill as a distinct, nameable event with visible data, so the sim labels every capture and shift instead of relying on ambient animation.

Implementation: p5.js, responsive canvas, mouse and touch drag support, window resize handler.

docs.title: Attention Regulation: The Operator, Not the Light
docs.text:
Now we can name the concept this whole book turns on. Attention regulation is the ability to direct attention where you intend it to go — to aim it, hold it, and move it on purpose rather than wherever the environment pulls it.

This distinction rescues families from a common dead end. People with ADHD do not have a shortage of attention. Anyone who has watched a twelve-year-old with ADHD play Minecraft for four unbroken hours, or an adult with ADHD rebuild a spreadsheet until 2 am, has seen attention in industrial quantities. What's inconsistent is the steering. Interest, novelty, urgency, and challenge grab the ADHD spotlight powerfully — sometimes too powerfully to break away from. Important-but-boring tasks barely tug at it, no matter how sincerely the person wants to do them.

Consider a worked example that plays out in thousands of homes. Maya, 24, spends Saturday afternoon deep in a coding side project — six hours, no breaks, forgets lunch. Sunday she needs forty minutes to renew her car registration online, and she cannot make herself start. Monday her mother calls, hears about the unrenewed registration, and thinks: she managed six hours for a hobby but not forty minutes for something that matters? The natural conclusion is that Maya doesn't care. The accurate conclusion is that Maya's attention steers toward interest and urgency, and away from tedium, far more strongly than her mother's does. The registration will likely get done in a panicked burst the day before the deadline — when urgency finally gives her spotlight something to lock onto.

If you have ADHD, learning your own steering patterns — what reliably grabs your attention, what reliably repels it — is the first practical skill in this book, and later chapters build systems around it. If you love someone with ADHD, this concept asks something specific of you: when effort looks wildly inconsistent, read it as a steering pattern to work with rather than a report on how much the person cares about you.

docs.title: Three Words the Diagnosis Is Built On
docs.text: The formal definition of ADHD, which we'll reach shortly, is built from three trait words: inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Each needs a careful definition, because each means something narrower and more specific than in everyday speech.

docs.title: Inattention
docs.text:
Inattention is the clinical name for a pattern of attention-regulation failures: losing the thread of tasks and conversations, drifting off during reading, missing details, losing objects, forgetting appointments, starting tasks and leaving them unfinished, and avoiding work that demands sustained mental effort. Notice what this list is made of — every item is a steering failure, which is why we defined attention regulation first.

Two things about inattention matter enormously for this book's readers. First, it's invisible. Hyperactivity announces itself; inattention just looks like an empty seat at the meeting, a lost permission slip, a bright student with a puzzling stack of missing assignments. Second, invisibility has a cost with a well-documented pattern: children whose ADHD is mostly inattentive — disproportionately girls — are diagnosed years later or never, because nobody is disrupted except them. A daydreaming girl who gets decent grades by being smart doesn't trigger anyone's alarm. She may spend twenty years being called an underachiever before anyone asks the right question. Chapter 4 returns to this at length.

A worked example. Two students take the same history class. Marcus calls out answers without raising his hand and can't stay in his seat; by October he has a file in the counselor's office. Elena sits quietly by the window, three chapters behind, reading the same paragraph for the fourth time because her mind keeps sliding off it. Her report card says "Elena is capable of so much more if she would only apply herself." Both students may have ADHD. One will be evaluated this year. The other may be evaluated at thirty-four, after her own child's diagnosis makes her recognize herself.

docs.title: Hyperactivity
docs.text:
Hyperactivity is excessive movement and restlessness beyond what fits the situation — the operative words being beyond what fits. All seven-year-olds run around; a hyperactive seven-year-old runs around during the fire drill, the spelling test, and dinner at grandma's, and can't stop when asked even when they genuinely try.

The word conjures a child, and that's a problem, because hyperactivity rarely disappears with age — it usually goes inside. The bouncing eight-year-old becomes a thirty-year-old with a jiggling knee, a chewed pen, three jobs' worth of commitments, and a mind that feels like a browser with forty tabs open. Adults with ADHD often describe being "driven by a motor" that idles too high: an inner restlessness that makes stillness genuinely uncomfortable. An adult who talks fast, fills every silence, can't relax on vacation, and volunteers for too much may be displaying hyperactivity as surely as the child on the furniture — but nobody sends a competent, busy adult for an evaluation, which is one more reason diagnosis so often comes late.

Worked example: at 9, Devon couldn't stay seated through a meal. At 39, Devon sits through hour-long meetings looking perfectly calm — while shredding a sticky note into confetti under the table, jaw tight from the effort of not interrupting, planning tonight's run because without a daily run his skin crawls. The hyperactivity didn't leave. It got a costume.

docs.title: Impulsivity
docs.text:
Impulsivity is acting before the thought that should have come first — answering before the question ends, grabbing, interrupting, deciding in seconds what deserves days. Between impulse and action, most brains insert a small pause where consequences get a hearing. Impulsivity is that pause failing to happen.

In children it looks like blurting, cutting in line, and snatching toys. In teens and adults the stakes rise: the sharp reply to a boss sent before rereading it, the purchase that empties the account, the lane change with no signal, the relationship-shaking sentence said in an argument and regretted within the minute. Impulsivity is also why later chapters treat driving, money, and conflict as safety topics rather than character topics.

One nuance both readers need: the person usually knows better. Ask them afterward and they can explain exactly why it was a bad idea — the knowledge was in the building, it just wasn't consulted in time. This gap between knowing and doing in the moment is a thread that runs through the entire book, and it's why "they know better, so they must have chosen this" is among the most damaging wrong conclusions a caregiver can draw. Punishing a knowledge gap that isn't there doesn't close the action gap that is.

Before the next section, explore how these three traits look at different ages — each trait card in this infographic shows the same trait wearing its child, teen, and adult costumes.
