A backpack problem that's working memory needs a launchpad by the door; one that's task initiation needs a smaller first step.

docs.title: The Chemistry: Dopamine, Norepinephrine, and the Reward System
docs.text:
Executive functions are the software; now two of the chemicals the hardware runs on. Neurons communicate using chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, and two of them dominate every serious conversation about ADHD — including, in Chapter 7, every serious conversation about medication.

Dopamine is the neurotransmitter most tied to motivation, reward anticipation, and salience — the brain's tagging system for this matters, move toward it. A crucial correction to pop culture: dopamine's main job in this story isn't pleasure itself so much as the pull toward things — the wanting, the drive, the surge when a reward looks likely. Dopamine signaling is central to the circuits that decide what's worth effort, and in ADHD those signals appear to run differently — weaker tagging for distant or mild rewards, stronger relative pull from immediate, novel, or intense ones. Chapter 1's video: "ADHD is just a dopamine deficiency you can fix" was wrong as a cure pitch, but it was built on a kernel of legitimate science — dopamine signaling differences do sit somewhere near the middle of ADHD. The honest version has no simple deficiency and no supplement fix.

Norepinephrine is dopamine's partner in the prefrontal cortex — a messenger governing alertness, arousal, and signal-to-noise: how sharply the important input stands out from background. Prefrontal circuits perform best in a middle band of norepinephrine (too little: foggy; too much: frazzled), and several ADHD medications — including the main non-stimulants — work primarily on this system. When Chapter 7 explains why stimulants calm rather than wire a person with ADHD, dopamine and norepinephrine are the two words doing the work.

The reward system is the brain circuit — heavily dopamine-driven, wired straight into the prefrontal cortex — that evaluates possible rewards, generates motivation toward them, and learns from outcomes. Think of it as the brain's internal economist, constantly pricing every option: what's this worth, how soon does it pay, what does it cost? The ADHD reward system prices time differently — and that single repricing, next section, explains more daily ADHD behavior than any other fact in this chapter.

docs.title: Motivation: The Economist's Broken Discount Rate
docs.text:
Everyone discounts the future a little: $100 today beats $110 in a year for most people. Delay aversion is the research finding that in ADHD this discounting runs much steeper — rewards lose their motivational value unusually fast as they move away in time, and waiting itself registers as actively unpleasant, something to be escaped. A reward three weeks out isn't slightly less motivating to an ADHD reward system; it's motivationally almost invisible.

This is the engine under motivation and ADHD — the observed pattern that ADHD motivation is inconsistent in a way effort-explanations can't predict but reward-math can. The worked example every family eventually lives: two assignments, identical difficulty. The first is due tomorrow — done tonight, in ninety focused minutes. The second is due in three weeks and worth half the grade — untouched for twenty days, then done in a panicked all-nighter... ninety focused minutes, the night before. Same student, same ability, same actual work. The only variable was when the reward (or consequence) arrived. Under effort-theory, this student is unmotivated — except the two ninety-minute sprints prove otherwise. Under reward-math, both performances are the same brain behaving completely consistently: it moves when payoff enters motivational range. Deadlines don't create the ability; they move the reward close enough to see.

Clinicians summarize the pattern with a memorable label: the interest-based nervous system, a term from clinician William Dodson describing what reliably activates ADHD motivation — interest, novelty, challenge, urgency, and often competition or an audience — as opposed to the importance-based activation (priorities, consequences, obligations) that neurotypical planning runs on. It's a clinical description rather than a formal neuroscience category, but families find it immediately usable: stop asking "how important is this?" (a currency the system barely accepts) and start asking "how can this become interesting, novel, urgent, or shared?" — currencies it pays out for every time. Body doubling, gamified chores, artificial deadlines: every trick in Chapter 9 is a currency exchange.

Try the economist's math yourself — the simulator below lets you set a reward's size and distance and watch its motivational price under both discount curves.

docs.title: Diagram: Reward Discounting Simulator
docs.text:
Run the Reward Discounting Simulator fullscreen

Reward Discounting Simulator

Type: microsim sim-id: reward-discounting-simulator Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Learning objective: Apply (L3, Bloom verb: demonstrate) delay discounting by manipulating a reward's size and delay and observing its motivational value under typical and ADHD-steep discount curves — then demonstrating which interventions restore motivational value.

Canvas layout: Responsive. Main area: a graph, x-axis = delay (now, 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 3 months), y-axis = motivational value (0-100). Controls below; infobox side panel.

Visual elements:

  • Two discount curves drawn from the same starting reward: typical (gray, gentle decline) and ADHD-steep (orange, rapid early collapse)
  • A draggable reward marker: the learner sets its size (marker height) and delay (horizontal position); the sim displays its computed motivational value under each curve, side by side with the gap labeled
  • A "motivation threshold" horizontal line: below it, the task doesn't start; the ADHD curve visibly crosses below threshold much earlier in time
  • Intervention chips the learner can click to apply: "Break into today-sized piece" (moves marker near zero delay), "Add body double / audience" (raises the curve), "Make it novel or a game" (raises the curve), "Artificial deadline tomorrow" (moves the consequence near) — each visibly restores the marker above threshold and the infobox explains the mechanism

Interactive controls:

  • Drag: reward marker (size and delay)
  • Buttons: the four intervention chips, individually toggleable
  • Toggle: show/hide typical curve for comparison
  • Preset scenarios dropdown: "Assignment due in 3 weeks", "Gym membership", "Saving for a car" — each places the marker and invites the learner to fix it

Data visibility requirements:

  • Stage 1: Show the reward's numeric motivational value under both curves at the chosen delay
  • Stage 2: Show the threshold crossing point in days for each curve
  • Stage 3: After each intervention chip, show the new value and a one-sentence mechanism ("urgency moved the payoff into range")
  • Final: Preset scenarios end with a summary of which interventions worked and why

Instructional rationale: An Apply objective needs parameter manipulation with visible consequences; letting the learner rescue a below-threshold task with named interventions rehearses the exact strategy logic Chapters 9-10 will formalize.

Implementation: p5.js, responsive, hyperbolic discount functions with different k parameters for the two curves.

docs.title: Arousal, and Why Stimulation Can Be Self-Medication
docs.text: One more regulation system completes the motivation picture. Arousal regulation is the brain's management of its own alertness level — keeping you in the zone where you're awake enough to engage but calm enough to stay organized. ADHD brains hold that zone poorly, sliding toward under-arousal (fog, boredom that borders on physical discomfort, sleepiness during slow tasks) and sometimes overshooting into frazzle. This reframes a lot of puzzling behavior as self-regulation: the child rocking his chair during silent reading, the adult who does her best work in a noisy café, the teen who leaves homework for the adrenaline of midnight — each is adding stimulation to climb out of under-arousal, medicating the arousal problem with the tools at hand. Chapter 9 turns this from accident into design: chosen background noise, movement breaks, and stimulation on purpose instead of stimulation by emergency.

docs.title: Sleep and the ADHD Brain
docs.text:
Sleep and the ADHD brain have a rough, two-directional relationship that families consistently underestimate. Direction one: ADHD disrupts sleep. A majority of people with ADHD report sleep problems — hardest of all, trouble getting to sleep, with many running a delayed body clock that isn't ready for sleep until well past midnight, plus a racing default mode network the moment the lights go off, plus "revenge bedtime procrastination": staying up because night is finally the quiet, demand-free time that never appeared during the day. Direction two: poor sleep worsens every symptom in this book. Sleep deprivation degrades exactly the prefrontal functions ADHD already strains — working memory, inhibition, emotional control — so a short night doesn't just add tiredness, it amplifies ADHD itself. Severe sleep deprivation can even mimic ADHD in people who don't have it, which is why competent evaluators (Chapter 5) always ask about sleep.

The worked example is a loop many households will recognize: Marcus, 16, can't settle until 1:30 am (delayed clock, racing mind), drags out of bed at 6:45, and runs the school day on five hours. His inhibition and working memory — already his hardest functions — perform at their worst; the day goes badly; the evening homework stretches late on a fried executive battery; the stress pushes sleep later still. His parents fight him about "staying up on his phone," which is real but downstream — the phone fills the wakefulness; it didn't create all of it. Treating Marcus's sleep as a first-class ADHD intervention rather than a discipline issue — a fixed wake time, light in the morning, and yes, boundaries on the phone, but framed as clock-repair rather than punishment — is often the single highest-leverage move a family can make, and Chapter 8 gives it a full section.

docs.title: Memory: Filing Versus Remembering-to-Do
docs.text:
ADHD and memory has a shape that surprises families: long-term memory — the filing cabinet of facts, events, and skills — is generally fine in ADHD. The person who "can't remember anything" recalls your first date, obscure movie dialogue, and an insult from 2014 in high fidelity. What actually fails are the two memory operations that route through executive systems: getting things into the files (working memory, the leaky desk you've met — information that never lands can't later be retrieved) and remembering at the right moment to act — which has its own name and its own budget line in this book.

Prospective memory is memory for intentions — remembering to do things at the moment they're due: take the medication at 8, bring the form Thursday, call mom back after this meeting, take out the trash before the truck comes. It differs from ordinary recall in one brutal way: nothing prompts it. Nobody asks "what were you supposed to do right now?" — the remembering has to fire by itself, at the right instant, unassisted. That self-firing depends on exactly the prefrontal machinery this chapter has been touring, and in ADHD it's among the most reliably impaired functions — especially time-based intentions ("at 3 pm") versus event-based ones ("when you see Dana").

Prospective memory failure is also the single greatest generator of relationship damage in ADHD families, because it's indistinguishable, from the outside, from not caring. The worked example: Sam (Chapter 1's Sam, still married) promises Tuesday morning to pick up his wife's prescription after work. He means it completely. At 5:15 he walks out of work into a phone call, drives home on autopilot, and the intention never fires — until her face at the door fires it instantly and sickeningly. She has an explanation available: if it mattered to him, he'd have remembered. You now have the hardware fact instead: the intention was filed and intact — what failed was the unprompted alarm, the least reliable component in his brain. The fix is never "promise harder." It's refusing to let any intention live only in a brain: the phone alarm set in her presence at the moment of promising, the pharmacy pinned to his drive-home route, the shared list. Chapter 9 builds this into a system with a name — externalizing memory — and Chapter 14 builds the family agreements around it.

docs.title: Cognitive Load: The Budget Everything Draws On
docs.text:
The last concept ties the chapter into one picture. Cognitive load is the total demand placed on working memory and executive systems at a given moment — every instruction held, decision pending, distraction resisted, and step tracked, all drawing on the same small budget. Everyone's budget is finite. ADHD's is smaller and drains faster — and, crucially, load is invisible, so observers routinely bill a person for failures of an overdrawn account they can't see.

Run the example: "empty the dishwasher" sounds like one task. Under load-accounting it's dozens of micro-decisions (where does this go? is this clean?) executed amid competing noise, on top of whatever the day already spent. On a fresh budget, trivial. At 9 pm, after a day of masking symptoms at school or work — an expense you'll meet properly in Chapter 4 — the same request can arrive at a genuinely empty account, and the response (snapping, shutdown, "I'll do it later" that never comes) reads as attitude. The load lens converts whole categories of family fight into engineering problems: reduce simultaneous demands, shrink decision counts, put instructions on paper instead of in RAM, and stop scheduling hard asks for empty-account hours. If Chapter 1's gift was the regulation lens, this chapter's is the load lens — and nearly every tool in Part Three of this book is, one way or another, a load-reduction device.

Check yourself: your daughter aced yesterday's history test but left today's permission slip — signed, on the counter, by the door — at home. Name the two memory systems involved and why the outcomes differ. Click to check.

The test drew on long-term memory — the filing cabinet, generally intact in ADHD. The slip needed prospective memory — remembering to act (grab it) at one specific unprompted moment (walking out), which routes through executive systems and is among ADHD's least reliable functions. High performance on one predicts nothing about the other; they're different machines. The fix is external: the slip goes in the backpack the moment it's signed, or a launchpad checklist lives on the door. (If you also said her working memory was busy with headphones-keys-lunch at exit time — cognitive load — full marks.)

docs.title: What to Carry Out of This Chapter
docs.text:
For the reader with ADHD:

  • Your struggles have addresses: initiation, working memory, prospective memory, delay-steep motivation, arousal, sleep. Naming the component is the first step to engineering around it — and you'll map your own profile in the Owner's Manual.
  • Your motivation runs on interest, novelty, urgency, and challenge. That's a system to design for, and every deadline-sprint you've ever pulled is evidence the ability was there all along.
  • Protect sleep and watch your load budget. Both quietly set the ceiling on everything else.

For the reader who loves someone with ADHD:

  • The maturation lag means age-typical expectations can be billing for hardware that isn't installed yet. Scaffold the gap; don't punish it.
  • The forgotten promise and the unstarted task are hardware events — prospective memory and task initiation — before they are statements about love or respect. Respond with external systems, made together, rather than louder reminders.
  • "He did it fine yesterday" is exactly what inconsistent regulation predicts. Variability is the symptom, not the proof of choice.

You now hold the machinery: a late-finishing prefrontal cortex running six executive functions on dopamine and norepinephrine, pricing rewards on a steep discount curve, with a small and drainable load budget. Chapter 3 uses this machinery to explain why ADHD comes in three different-looking presentations — and why two people with the same diagnosis can look nothing alike.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Applied Quiz: The ADHD Brain
docs.text: A second set of questions on this chapter, weighted toward applying the ideas rather than recalling them. Each one gives you a situation and asks which piece of the machinery explains it.

docs.title: 1. A manager says: "Before the meeting, print the deck, use Dana's updated numbers, and book the small room." The employee arrives with the deck, old numbers, no room. Which executive function was overloaded?
docs.text:
1. Working memory — three sequential verbal instructions exceeded the mental desk, so the later items shoved out the earlier ones
  2. Response inhibition — she failed to suppress a competing action
  3. Cognitive flexibility — she could not shift between the three sub-tasks
  4. Self-monitoring — she did not notice she was drifting off task
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. This is the chapter's Priya example. Working memory is the small workspace holding information while you use it, and three sequential spoken instructions exceeded it — the second shoved out the first, a hallway greeting shoved out the third. The information was never filed, so this isn't forgetting in the filing-cabinet sense. Options B, C, and D name real executive functions, but none describes an overloaded capacity limit. Note the practical consequence: the fix is never "listen harder," it's writing things down as they arrive, because paper has no capacity limit.

Concept Tested: Working Memory

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 2. A student does a hard assignment due tomorrow in ninety focused minutes, but leaves a bigger assignment due in three weeks untouched for twenty days — then does it in ninety focused minutes the night before. What does reward-math conclude?
docs.text:
1. The student is unmotivated, and the two sprints were flukes
  2. The student has a skills gap that panic temporarily closes
  3. The two assignments differed in difficulty despite appearances
  4. The same brain behaved consistently — it moved when the payoff came close enough to enter motivational range
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter uses exactly this case to contrast effort-theory with reward-math. Under effort-theory the student looks unmotivated, except the two identical ninety-minute sprints prove otherwise. Under reward-math both performances are the same brain behaving consistently: the only variable was when the consequence arrived. Deadlines don't create the ability — they move the reward close enough to see. Options A and B misread the sprints as exceptions rather than as the evidence. Option C contradicts the setup, which holds difficulty constant.

Concept Tested: Delay Aversion

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 3. An adult writes well and handles hard emails in the morning, then by late afternoon rereads paragraphs, snaps at a coworker, and impulse-buys a gadget. What is the best explanation?
docs.text:
1. Two different conditions are at work, one affecting mornings and one affecting afternoons
  2. Prefrontal work is expensive and depletes with fatigue, so the same person is running on a drained executive battery
  3. Her ADHD is intermittent, which rules out a neurodevelopmental explanation
  4. The afternoon behavior reflects a character problem the morning conceals
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Every item on that list — sustained attention, inhibiting the snap, resisting the impulse buy — is prefrontal, and the prefrontal cortex is the brain's heaviest lifting, easily depleted by fatigue, stress, hunger, and poor sleep. As the chapter puts it about Aisha: the machine didn't change, the fuel gauge did. Option D is the character reading the chapter is written to replace. Option A invents a second condition. Option C mistakes a predictable daily pattern for evidence against a lifelong condition.

Concept Tested: Prefrontal Cortex

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 4. Parents of a 13-year-old point out that his classmates manage their own backpacks. Using the maturation-lag finding, what is the flaw in that comparison?
docs.text:
1. There is no flaw — same-age peers are the correct benchmark
  2. The comparison is unfair because backpack management is not an executive function
  3. They are right that peers manage it, but wrong about what hardware he is running — the organizing circuitry may be on a schedule closer to a 10-year-old's
  4. Brain scans could settle the question for this specific child
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's Leo example makes exactly this move: his body, vocabulary, and height are 13, so everyone bills him for 13-year-old self-management, but the circuitry that inhibits impulses and organizes homework may run on a younger schedule. The useful question becomes what scaffolding bridges the gap while it narrows. Option D is ruled out explicitly — the lag is a group average, and no brain scan can diagnose ADHD in an individual. Option B is wrong: organizing a backpack is planning and working memory.

Concept Tested: ADHD Brain Maturation Lag

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 5. A clinic advertises brain scans that "diagnose ADHD definitively." How should a family evaluate this offer?
docs.text:
1. Decline — neuroimaging findings in ADHD are consistent at the group level, but no scan can diagnose an individual, so the clinic is selling past the evidence
  2. Accept, since imaging is more objective than rating scales and interviews
  3. Accept only if the scan is read alongside a genetic test
  4. Decline, because no reliable group-level brain differences have been found in ADHD
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter says this plainly and points readers back to Chapter 1's five-question filter. Group-level findings are real — the maturation delay, small average volume differences in childhood, differences in network coordination — but they do not transfer to individual diagnosis. Option D overcorrects and denies findings that genuinely exist. Options B and C treat imaging as more authoritative than the clinical assessment described in Chapter 5.

Concept Tested: Neuroimaging Findings

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 6. A child rocks his chair during silent reading, an adult works best in a noisy café, and a teen saves homework for midnight adrenaline. What single mechanism links all three?
docs.text:
1. Avoidance — each is a way of escaping a disliked task
  2. Response inhibition failing in three different settings
  3. Poor sleep hygiene expressing itself at different ages
  4. Arousal regulation — each is adding stimulation to climb out of under-arousal, self-medicating with the tools at hand
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter reframes all three as self-regulation rather than misbehavior: ADHD brains hold the alert-but-organized zone poorly and slide toward under-arousal, where boredom borders on physical discomfort. Chapter 9 turns this from accident into design — chosen background noise, movement breaks, stimulation on purpose instead of by emergency. Option A misreads deliberate stimulation-seeking as avoidance. Option B names the brake, which isn't what's operating. Option C explains only the midnight case, and not why café noise helps.

Concept Tested: Arousal Regulation

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 7. A reader is midway through a page and suddenly realizes they have spent three minutes mentally rewriting an argument from 2019, with no memory of leaving the page. Which finding names this?
docs.text:
1. Working memory overflow during reading
  2. Unreliable suppression of the default mode network, so the brain's screensaver flickers back on mid-task
  3. Delay aversion applied to long-form text
  4. A failure of the brake, since the thought should have been inhibited
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. On-task brains normally suppress the default mode network — the network handling daydreaming, remembering, and replaying conversations — and in ADHD that suppression is less reliable. The chapter offers this exact experience as the inside view. It also notes the flip side: that idling network is where unexpected connections and creative leaps come from, a thread Chapter 11 picks up. Options A, C, and D name mechanisms that don't describe an intruding internal-thought network.

Concept Tested: Default Mode Network

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 8. A family wants to motivate a teenager toward a chore that is important but dull. Which approach fits the interest-based nervous system?
docs.text:
1. Explain more clearly how important the chore is and what depends on it
  2. Increase the consequence for not doing it, so the obligation registers
  3. Convert the chore into a currency the system pays out for — make it novel, urgent, shared, or competitive
  4. Wait until the teenager matures enough for importance to work
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's practical translation is to stop asking "how important is this?" — a currency the system barely accepts — and start asking how it can become interesting, novel, urgent, or shared. Body doubling, gamified chores, and artificial deadlines are all currency exchanges, and Chapter 9 is built from them. Options A and B keep paying in the importance currency that doesn't convert. Option D misreads a lifespan pattern as something waiting to resolve on its own.

Concept Tested: Interest-Based Nervous System

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 9. A teenager sleeps five hours nightly during exam season and her ADHD symptoms visibly worsen. What does the chapter's two-directional account predict?
docs.text:
1. Sleep loss adds tiredness but leaves ADHD symptoms themselves unchanged
  2. The worsening indicates the ADHD diagnosis was probably wrong
  3. Sleep and ADHD are largely independent, so the timing is coincidental
  4. Sleep loss degrades the same prefrontal functions ADHD already strains, so it doesn't just add tiredness — it amplifies ADHD itself
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The relationship runs both ways: ADHD disrupts sleep (delayed body clock, racing default mode network at lights-out, revenge bedtime procrastination), and poor sleep degrades working memory, inhibition, and emotional control — exactly the functions already under strain. The chapter adds a detail worth carrying: severe sleep deprivation can even mimic ADHD in people who don't have it, which is why competent evaluators always ask about sleep. Options A and C deny the amplification. Option B inverts the logic.

Concept Tested: Sleep And The ADHD Brain

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 10. Two adults both have ADHD. One cannot begin tasks but manages instructions easily; the other starts instantly but cannot let go of a failed approach. What does this tell you about strategy?
docs.text:
1. One of them has been misdiagnosed, since ADHD presents consistently
  2. Executive functions are distinct, so profiles differ — and strategies attach to specific components rather than to "ADHD" in general
  3. The difference reflects effort, not machinery
  4. They need identical strategies, since both have the same underlying condition
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter states this directly before the explorer: executive functions are distinct, so one person's working memory can be fine while initiation is wrecked, and another launches instantly but can't shift gears. This is why Chapter 15's Personal Owner's Manual asks readers to map their own profile, and why the strategies in Chapters 9 and 10 attach to named components. A backpack problem that is working memory needs a launchpad by the door; one that is task initiation needs a smaller first step. Options A and D assume a uniformity the chapter denies; option C returns to the effort explanation.

Concept Tested: Executive Function

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: Quiz: The ADHD Brain
docs.text: Test your understanding of brain development, executive function, dopamine, and motivation in ADHD with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is executive function, as this chapter defines it?
docs.text:
1. The umbrella term for the mental skills that manage other skills, such as starting tasks, holding information in mind, and inhibiting impulses
  2. A single brain region that controls movement
  3. Another name for long-term memory
  4. The medical term for hyperactivity
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Executive function is the umbrella name for the mental skills the prefrontal systems provide — skills that manage other skills, like starting a task, holding instructions in mind, and resisting distraction. Option B confuses it with a motor region. Option C is wrong because long-term memory is generally intact in ADHD and is a separate system. Option D mislabels a set of cognitive skills as a single symptom.

Concept Tested: Executive Function

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 2. According to this chapter, which brain region matures last, often not finishing until the mid-to-late twenties?
docs.text:
1. The visual cortex
  2. The cerebellum
  3. The default mode network
  4. The prefrontal cortex
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter explains that the prefrontal cortex — the region handling planning, self-control, and judgment — is the last major brain area to finish developing, running into the mid-to-late twenties. The visual cortex and movement-related regions mature much earlier. The default mode network is a functional network, not the late-maturing region itself.

Concept Tested: Prefrontal Cortex

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 3. What is working memory, as described in this chapter?
docs.text:
1. The brain's permanent storage for facts and events
  2. The small mental workspace that holds information while it's being used, such as an instruction while carrying it out
  3. The system that controls physical balance
  4. A synonym for long-term memory
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter describes working memory as "the mental desk" — a small workspace that holds information while it is actively being used, illustrated by Priya losing instructions mid-errand. Options A and D describe long-term memory, a separate and generally intact system in ADHD. Option C describes an unrelated physical function.

Concept Tested: Working Memory

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 4. What is prospective memory?
docs.text:
1. Memory for facts learned in school
  2. Memory for people's names
  3. Memory for intentions — remembering to do something at the right future moment, without a prompt
  4. Memory that improves with age
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Prospective memory is memory for intentions — remembering to act at the right moment, such as taking medication or picking up a prescription, with nothing external prompting the recall. Options A and B describe long-term memory for facts or names, a different system. Option D is not a claim the chapter makes.

Concept Tested: Prospective Memory

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 5. According to the chapter's discussion of delay aversion and the interest-based nervous system, what activates motivation most reliably in ADHD?
docs.text:
1. Interest, novelty, urgency, and challenge
  2. Long-term importance and moral obligation
  3. Careful step-by-step planning
  4. Rewards that are distant but large
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter describes the ADHD brain as running on an "interest-based nervous system," activated reliably by interest, novelty, challenge, and urgency, rather than by importance alone. Option B describes the importance-based activation that neurotypical planning relies on. Option C describes a planning skill, not a motivational trigger. Option D is contradicted by delay aversion, which makes distant rewards lose motivational pull fast.

Concept Tested: Interest-Based Nervous System

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 6. What does the chapter say happens to the default mode network during focused tasks in ADHD, and what is the consequence?
docs.text:
1. It shuts off completely and never activates
  2. It only activates in people without ADHD
  3. It has no connection to attention at all
  4. It is suppressed less reliably during tasks, so daydreaming intrudes mid-task
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter explains that the default mode network normally gets suppressed when focused work begins, but in ADHD that suppression is less reliable, so the mind wanders back into it mid-task — the "screensaver" flickering on. Options A and C misdescribe the network as inactive or irrelevant. Option B is false; everyone's default mode network activates during idle moments.

Concept Tested: Default Mode Network

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 7. Which statement correctly interprets the ADHD brain maturation lag finding?
docs.text:
1. It proves that any individual child with ADHD is exactly three years behind peers on a brain scan
  2. It is a group-average finding showing delayed but similarly shaped cortical development, with some differences persisting into adulthood
  3. It means ADHD is fully outgrown once the brain catches up around age 25
  4. It shows brain scans can reliably diagnose ADHD in an individual
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter is explicit that the maturation lag is a group-average research finding — cortical development follows the same route on a delayed timetable — and that some differences persist into adulthood, which is why ADHD is a lifespan condition. Option A over-applies a group statistic to an individual. Option C contradicts the chapter's point that the lag doesn't mean full catch-up. Option D is directly rejected: no scan can diagnose an individual.

Concept Tested: ADHD Brain Maturation Lag

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 8. What is cognitive load, and why does the chapter emphasize it?
docs.text:
1. It is a measure of IQ that predicts ADHD severity
  2. It is fixed and identical for everyone regardless of the day
  3. It is the total demand on working memory and executive systems at a given moment, and it is invisible, so people get blamed for failures of a budget they've already overdrawn
  4. It only affects people without ADHD
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Cognitive load is the total demand on working memory and executive systems at any moment, and the chapter stresses that because load is invisible, observers often blame a person for failures caused by an already-overdrawn budget, as in the dishwasher example. Option A confuses it with intelligence. Option B contradicts the chapter's point that load varies by time of day and prior demands. Option D is false; load affects everyone, just with a smaller and faster-draining budget in ADHD.

Concept Tested: Cognitive Load

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 9. Ben sits down at his desk wanting to start his tax return, but twenty minutes pass and he still hasn't opened the file, even though he understands exactly what to do. Which executive function does this scenario best illustrate failing?
docs.text:
1. Task initiation
  2. Working memory
  3. Cognitive flexibility
  4. Self-monitoring
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. This matches the chapter's description of task initiation as "the starter motor" — converting intention into the first action — where a person can want to start, know exactly what to do, and still be unable to launch. Working memory (B) concerns holding information in mind, not starting. Cognitive flexibility (C) concerns shifting between tasks or approaches. Self-monitoring (D) concerns tracking ongoing performance, not beginning it.

Concept Tested: Task Initiation

See: Chapter 2

docs.title: 10. Sam forgets to pick up his wife's prescription despite promising that morning; his wife concludes "if it mattered to him, he'd have remembered." Which option best analyzes what actually failed, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Sam's long-term memory failed, since he couldn't recall the promise at all
  2. Sam never truly formed the intention, so nothing failed
  3. Sam's prospective memory failed — the intention was intact, but the brain's unprompted, self-firing alarm at the right moment didn't fire
  4. Sam's working memory was overloaded at the moment he made the promise
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter analyzes this exact example as a prospective memory failure: the intention was filed and genuine, but the unprompted, self-triggered alarm that should have fired at 5:15 didn't, which looks identical to not caring from the outside. Option A misidentifies the memory system involved. Option B contradicts the chapter's claim that Sam meant it completely. Option D misplaces the failure at the moment of promising rather than at the moment of action.

Concept Tested: Prospective Memory

See: Chapter 2

  2. Prefrontal cortex - Wikipedia - Anatomy and function of the brain's executive suite, including its long maturation timeline — the biology behind this chapter's construction-schedule story.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the three official presentations of ADHD and the everyday traits families actually recognize: hyperfocus, time blindness, procrastination, forgetfulness, and the inconsistency that confuses everyone. It also introduces masking — working hard to look fine — which matters for the chapters ahead. After this chapter, readers can name what they are seeing instead of arguing about it.
