docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter begins the practical toolkit: externalizing memory instead of trusting it, breaking tasks down, estimating time, using timers, body doubling, and building routines that fit an ADHD brain. These are the daily mechanics that turn understanding into a better Tuesday. After this chapter, readers have a starter set of systems to try.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept CIS Score Externalizing Memory 32 Capture Systems 6 To-Do Lists That Work 3 Task Breakdown 2 Defining Next Actions 1 Time Estimation 4 Timers And Alarms 2 Pomodoro Technique 1 Body Doubling 4 Accountability Partners 3 Routines And Habits 8 Habit Stacking 1 Morning Routines 1 Evening Routines 1 Environment Design 9

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: The ADHD Brain
  • Chapter 3: Presentations And Everyday Traits
  • Chapter 8: Treatment Beyond Medication

Eight chapters of understanding now get cashed in. Everything here follows one engineering rule, derived from everything you know: stop asking the brain to do what it's bad at, and move that work into the world. Working memory leaks — so put information on paper. Prospective memory misfires — so let alarms do the firing. Time is invisible — so make it visible. Starting is the hard part — so shrink the start. None of these systems requires becoming a different person; that's the point of them.

Two ground rules before the toolkit. First, systems beat willpower — Chapter 1's willpower myth retired trying-harder as a strategy, and this chapter is what replaced it. Second, expect iteration: the first version of any system will half-work, and per Chapter 3's variability, a system that fails on Tuesday may fit fine with one adjustment. Tinkering is the method, not a sign of failure. For the family reader: your role throughout this chapter is collaborator and occasional infrastructure — never enforcement. A system imposed on a person with ADHD is a nag with laminations; a system built with them is scaffolding they'll actually stand on. Chapter 14 draws these lines carefully; keep them in view all chapter.

docs.title: The Master Principle: Externalizing Memory
docs.text:
Externalizing memory means moving information out of your head and into reliable external storage — paper, phone, whiteboard, alarm, a bowl by the door — the moment it arrives. It's the master principle because it directly patches the two most reliable failure points from Chapter 2: working memory (the leaky desk — information never encoded can't be recalled) and prospective memory (the alarm that doesn't fire — intentions kept "in mind" don't surface on schedule). The rule in its usable form: if it matters, it doesn't live in your head. Not the appointment, not the promise to your wife, not the great idea in the shower, not "I'll bring the form Thursday." Heads are for having thoughts, not holding them.

The worked example is Chapter 2's Sam, re-run with the system installed. Tuesday morning, Sam promises to pick up the prescription. At the moment of promising — this timing is the whole trick — he sets a 5:05 pm phone alarm labeled "PHARMACY before home," in front of his wife. At 5:05 the alarm fires as he's walking out into the same distracting phone call as before; the label steers the drive. Nothing about Sam's brain changed between the two versions of this story. The intention was moved from the least reliable storage he owns (prospective memory) to the most reliable (a device that never forgets and interrupts on schedule). His wife's part also changed: instead of testing his love nightly against his weakest brain function, she watched him build the alarm — which reads as the promise being taken seriously, because it is. Externalization done at the moment of commitment is what taking-it-seriously looks like in an ADHD household.

docs.title: Capture, Lists, and the Art of Starting
docs.text:
Capture systems are externalization's front door: one always-available place where every incoming commitment, idea, and obligation lands the instant it appears — before working memory can drop it. The operative word is one: five capture points (a notebook here, three apps, a sticky note ecosystem) recreate the original problem as "which list was that on?" Pick the tool that is always physically present (for most people, the phone's notes or reminders app; for some, a pocket notebook or a kitchen whiteboard for household items) and grant it a monopoly. The capture habit itself — reaching for it mid-conversation, at the mailbox, in the parking lot — feels rude and mechanical for about two weeks, and then it quietly removes a whole category of failure. Families: when your person pauses a conversation to capture, that's the system working; the respectful move is to wait, not to add two more items while they type.

To-do lists that work are what capture becomes after a nightly two-minute sort, and the ADHD-specific engineering matters because standard list advice fails this population predictably. Three rules fix most of it. Keep today's list to three-to-five items and physically separate from the everything-list — a forty-item list is Chapter 3's decision paralysis printed out, and its daily non-completion is a shame generator (Chapter 11 cares about this). Write items as actions, not topics (next paragraph). And put the list where the eyes already go — taped to the monitor, on the lock screen — because a list that must be remembered-to-be-checked dies by the very failure mode it was built to fix.

Task breakdown attacks the paralysis in front of big vague tasks — Chapter 2's map-maker function, outsourced to a calmer moment. "Clean the garage," "apply to colleges," "do taxes" are not tasks; they're projects wearing a task's name, fifty invisible steps with no marked entrance. The technique: split any project into steps small enough that no single step is scary — and if a step still produces the avoidance feeling, split that step. Defining next actions is the breakdown's cutting edge and the single highest-value habit in this section: for anything stalled, name the physically next thing — not "work on taxes" but "find last year's return in the email and download it." Concrete, small, start-able in under ten minutes. The test of a real next action is that you could do it right now without deciding anything further. Most "procrastination" on projects (Chapter 3 absolved the character; this is the mechanism) is actually an undefined next action: the starter motor has nothing its size to grab. A worked example in one line: "renew the car registration" sat for three weeks; "find the renewal notice on the counter and put it by the laptop" took ninety seconds and broke the dam — because the ninety-second version asked nothing of planning, only of doing.

docs.title: Diagram: Next-Action Trainer
docs.text:
Run the Next-Action Trainer fullscreen

Next-Action Trainer

Type: microsim sim-id: next-action-trainer Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Learning objective: Create (L6, Bloom verb: formulate) proper next actions by decomposing vague stalled tasks into concrete, immediately startable steps, and judging candidate actions against the "startable now, no further decisions" test.

Canvas layout: Responsive. Left/top: a "stalled task" card. Right/bottom: workspace and feedback panel.

Modes:

  1. Judge mode: shows a stalled task ("apply for the internship") and four candidate next actions of varying quality ("work on application", "think about essay topics", "open the portal and screenshot the requirements list", "be more organized about deadlines"); learner picks the real next action; feedback names the test each failed candidate flunks (topic-not-action, requires further decisions, not physically specifiable, character-goal-not-action)
  2. Build mode: shows a vague project ("clean the garage", "plan grandma's birthday", "fix the resume") and a free-text field; learner writes their own next action; the sim checks it against heuristics (starts with a verb, mentions a specific object/place, estimated under 10 minutes via a self-rated slider) and gives rubric-style feedback rather than right/wrong
  3. Chain mode: after a valid next action, asks "and after that?" three times, demonstrating that chains are built one link at a time and only the first link needs to exist today

Content pool: at least 12 stalled tasks spanning home, school, work, and family life, several drawn from the book's running examples (registration renewal, the taxes, the college applications).

Interactive controls: Mode selector, task shuffle, a "still scary? split it again" button in build mode that prompts a smaller re-write.

Data visibility requirements: Feedback always names the specific heuristic passed or failed; a summary screen collects the learner's built actions into a copyable list formatted like the chapter's today-list (3-5 items max, action-phrased).

Instructional rationale: Formulating next actions is a generative skill — a Create-level objective — so the sim centers free construction with rubric feedback, using judge mode only as the on-ramp.

Implementation: p5.js with HTML input overlay for text entry; responsive; heuristic checks are keyword/length/slider-based, deliberately forgiving.

docs.title: Making Time Visible
docs.text:
Time estimation — the skill time blindness (Chapter 3) degrades — improves with one mechanical practice: measure, don't vibe. The technique is an estimation log: before a recurring task, write the guess; after, write the actual; review weekly. Dana's eight-minute getting-ready belief (Chapter 3) survives only because it's never confronted with data — three logged mornings reveal it's twenty-six minutes, and the revised number, not self-scolding, is what changes the departure math. Two rules of thumb while calibration builds: multiply gut estimates for boring multi-step tasks by 1.5 to 2, and schedule backward from hard deadlines using the logged numbers ("leave at 6:00" becomes "shower at 5:20," alarm set accordingly — at the start of the sequence, where Chapter 3 said it belongs).

Timers and alarms are prospective memory outsourced, and the difference between the two is worth one sentence: alarms fire at clock times (take the medication, leave for pickup, start winding down), while timers make durations visible and finite. Uses beyond the obvious: the transition warning ("five more minutes" made real, paying Chapter 3's transition tax in advance), the wear-off alarm (Chapter 7's 5 pm cliff, scheduled around), and the visible countdown — analog or app — that turns abstract time into a shrinking shape the eyes can check. Label every alarm with its action ("PHARMACY before home"), because an unlabeled 5:05 alarm two hours after setting it is a mystery, not an instruction.

The Pomodoro technique packages timers into a work rhythm: commit to one task for a fixed sprint (classically 25 minutes), take a short timed break (5), repeat; every few cycles, a longer break. Why it fits this brain specifically: the sprint is small enough for the starter motor (you're not starting the thesis, you're starting 25 minutes), the ticking countdown supplies urgency the deadline is too far away to provide (Chapter 2's discount curve, artificially steepened), and the sanctioned break gives restlessness a legal exit instead of a guilty one. ADHD adaptations that practitioners converge on: tune the sprint length to your actual attention (some do better at 15, some at 45 — the log tells you), guard the break's end with its own alarm (the break is where Pomodoro dies), and if hyperfocus arrives mid-sprint on the right task, let it run — the technique is a starter, not a governor.

docs.title: Borrowing Other People's Presence
docs.text:
Body doubling is the strategy with the strangest name and the most devoted users: doing your work in the presence of another person who is simply there — working on their own things, not helping, not supervising. The wife reading while you do taxes; the friend on a video call, each muted, doing separate chores; a café's ambient population. Why mere presence works maps onto Chapter 2: another person supplies mild arousal (climbing out of the under-stimulated fog), a whiff of social accountability (someone would notice you wandering off), and interest-currency (even boring tasks become slightly performed). It costs nothing and converts some people's worst task categories from impossible to routine — which makes it the first thing to try on any chronically stalled chore. For the family reader, note what body doubling asks of you and what it doesn't: sit nearby with your own book — and resist narrating, correcting, or supervising, which converts a body double into a foreman and cancels the effect.

Accountability partners are the scheduled version of the same physics: a specific person expecting a specific thing at a specific time — the gym friend at 7 am, the Sunday "did we both do our admin?" text, the writing group's Friday pages. The mechanism is external deadline manufacture: the reward system that ignores "someday" responds to "Casey is standing outside at 7." Design rules learned the hard way: make the commitment concrete and dated (not "let's keep each other on track"), keep stakes friendly (shame-based accountability gets avoided along with the task — the partner you start dodging has become a second deadline problem), and prefer peers over spouses for recurring task accountability, because Chapter 14 will have strong opinions about what chronic monitor-roles do to a marriage.

docs.title: Routines: Automating the Decisions Away
docs.text:
Routines and habits matter to this brain for a reason Chapter 2 makes precise: every decision spends load, and a routine is a decision eliminator — the sequence runs on rails, so the executive budget stays unspent for things that deserve it. The honest ADHD caveat comes first: habits form more slowly and break more easily with ADHD (interest fades, one disrupted week derails the rails), so the design rules below matter more here than for other brains, and a collapsed routine is a Tuesday event to be re-started, not a character verdict. The rules: anchor every routine to an existing fixed event rather than a clock time ("after the coffee finishes" survives weekends; "at 7:15" doesn't); keep chains short (three-to-five steps — long routines fail at their weakest link); externalize the sequence itself (a checklist on the bathroom mirror is the routine's memory, so the head doesn't have to be); and rebuild shrunk, not bigger, after a collapse (the two-step version that runs beats the seven-step version that doesn't).

Habit stacking is the anchoring rule as a technique: attach a new habit directly onto an existing automatic one — after I pour the coffee, I take the medication; after I take the medication, I check the today-list. The existing habit becomes the cue, which is exactly the externalization principle again — the trigger lives in the environment's sequence, not in remembering. Stack one new link at a time; a five-link stack installed in one motivated weekend is a Chapter 3 abandoned-hobby story waiting to happen.

Morning routines deserve their own engineering because mornings are the day's cascade point — a derailed morning taxes everything after it — and because mornings run on the day's least medicated, least caffeinated, most rushed brain. The ADHD-specific move: shift every possible decision to the night before (clothes chosen, bag packed, breakfast planned, keys in the bowl), so the morning is pure execution on rails. Keep the live sequence stupid-simple and posted where it happens. Evening routines are the morning's supply line plus the sleep-protection front line from Chapters 6 and 8: a launchpad ritual (bag, keys, forms, tomorrow's three-item list — five minutes that de-mine the morning) followed by a wind-down with its own start alarm, because the night's real enemy is the un-decided drift into one-more-episode. The pair works as a loop: the evening routine is genuinely the morning routine's first half.

docs.title: Environment Design: The Room Is Part of the Brain
docs.text:
Environment design is the principle underneath half this chapter, promoted to a strategy: since the environment steers the spotlight more than intention does (Chapter 1), arrange the environment to do the steering you want. Its two operating rules point in opposite directions. Add friction to the wrong things: the phone charges in the kitchen during homework (the capture that can't happen), the game controller lives in a drawer across the room, the snacks aren't at the desk. Remove friction from the right things: the gym bag packed by the door, the vitamin bottle on the coffee maker, the guitar on a wall hook instead of in a case, the form already clipped to the clipboard with a pen. Each moved object is a decision pre-made and a temptation pre-blocked — willpower stored in furniture. Two applications tie the chapter's threads together: give every routinely-lost object a single home (Chapter 3's losing-things fix — the bowl, the hook, the charger spot — locations doing the remembering), and build visual triggers for anything that must happen (the trash by the front door on trash night; out of sight is genuinely out of mind for this brain, so put things in sight on purpose). A worked example at household scale: Rosa's family (Chapter 3) stopped relitigating her forgetting and spent one Saturday on infrastructure — key bowl by the door, charger shelf, a launchpad table, the shared whiteboard for household captures, alarms installed for the recurring three. Cost: an afternoon and $40. Effect: the four most common fights now have no occasion. Nobody's brain changed; the house got smarter.

Here's the starter set, collected — every row explained above:

System Fixes First step tonight One capture point Working memory leaks Pick the tool; grant it a monopoly Today-list (3-5 actions) List paralysis and shame Sort capture into tomorrow's three Next actions Stalled projects Name one ninety-second first step Estimation log Time blindness Guess-then-time one recurring task Labeled alarms Prospective memory Set the medication and departure alarms Pomodoro sprints Task initiation One 25-minute sprint, break alarm set Body double The impossible chore Schedule one co-working hour Habit stack Routine building Attach one new link to the coffee Launchpad + wind-down alarm Chaotic mornings, stolen sleep Five-minute evening reset tonight Object homes + friction moves Lost things, phone spirals The bowl, the hook, the kitchen charger

For both readers

Pick one row each — the person with ADHD chooses theirs, the family member chooses one for their own life (these systems are just good engineering; using them yourself beats prescribing them). Run both for two weeks before adding anything. The classic failure mode of this chapter is installing all ten systems in one inspired weekend and abandoning the wreckage by Thursday — that's Chapter 3's novelty curve, and the counter-move is boring, deliberate one-at-a-time.

Check yourself: 'I bought her a beautiful planner and she used it for nine days. She just won't stick to anything.' Diagnose with this chapter. Click to check.

Several mechanisms, no character required. (1) The planner was likely given, not co-built — imposed systems become laminated nags. (2) A planner is five systems in one (capture, lists, calendar, breakdown, review) — installed all at once, the classic collapse pattern the chapter warns about. (3) Paper planners must be remembered-to-be-checked — they die by the exact prospective-memory failure they're meant to fix, unless placed in a forced sightline or paired with an alarm. (4) Nine days is the novelty curve expiring on schedule; the fix is anchoring the check to an existing habit (stack: after coffee, open planner), not re-motivating. (5) A collapsed system gets rebuilt shrunk — maybe just the today-list on the lock screen — not re-imposed whole. And the "won't stick to anything" framing is Chapter 1's willpower myth; nine days of use is evidence of effort meeting an unengineered tool.

docs.title: What to Carry Out of This Chapter
docs.text:
For the reader with ADHD:

  • If it matters, it doesn't live in your head. Capture at the moment of arrival, alarm at the moment of promising.
  • Stalled means the next action is undefined or too big. Name the ninety-second version and split anything still scary.
  • Start one system, anchored to an existing habit, and expect to rebuild it smaller after it collapses. Rebuilding is the skill.

For the reader who loves someone with ADHD:

  • Build systems with, never for — and use a few yourself; shared infrastructure beats prescribed infrastructure.
  • Your presence is a tool: body doubling helps, foreman mode cancels it. Sit nearby with your own book.
  • When a system collapses, the useful sentence is "want to restart the small version together?" — not an audit of day nine.

Chapter 10 extends the toolkit into planners, calendars, apps, and the maintenance question nobody warns you about: what to do when every system you build eventually stops working — and why that's normal.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Applied Quiz: Building Daily Systems
docs.text: A second set of questions on this chapter, weighted toward applying the ideas rather than recalling them. Each one hands you a broken system and asks what the chapter would change.

docs.title: 1. A husband promises to pick up a prescription and forgets, for the third time. What does the chapter's master principle prescribe, and when?
docs.text:
1. A labeled alarm set at the moment of promising, in front of his wife — externalization done at the moment of commitment
  2. A firm reminder from his wife at 4:30, when it becomes urgent
  3. A written note left on the counter that evening
  4. A discussion about why the pharmacy keeps slipping his mind
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The timing is the whole trick. Sam sets a 5:05 alarm labeled "PHARMACY before home" at the moment of promising, and when it fires he is walking into the same distracting phone call as the failed version — but the label steers the drive. Nothing about his brain changed; the intention moved from his least reliable storage to his most reliable. The chapter adds a second effect: his wife watched him build the alarm, which reads as the promise being taken seriously, because it is.

Concept Tested: Externalizing Memory

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 2. Someone keeps a notebook, two apps, and a sticky-note system for capturing commitments, and still loses things. What is the fix?
docs.text:
1. Add a weekly consolidation step to merge all four
  2. Choose better apps with stronger features
  3. Grant one always-present tool a monopoly — five capture points recreate the original problem as "which list was that on?"
  4. Keep all four but assign each a category of commitment
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The operative word in the chapter's definition of capture systems is one. Pick the tool that is always physically present — for most people the phone's notes or reminders app, for some a pocket notebook or a kitchen whiteboard — and give it a monopoly. Options A and D preserve the multiplicity and add sorting work on top of it. Note the related family instruction: when someone pauses a conversation to capture, the respectful move is to wait, not to add two more items while they type.

Concept Tested: Capture Systems

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 3. A forty-item to-do list goes uncompleted every single day, and its owner feels worse each evening. Which three rules does the chapter apply?
docs.text:
1. Prioritize by importance, review monthly, and archive completed items
  2. Keep today's list to three-to-five items separate from the everything-list, write items as actions rather than topics, and put the list where the eyes already go
  3. Break every item into subtasks so progress is always visible
  4. Delete anything untouched for a week
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Standard list advice fails this population predictably, so the ADHD-specific engineering matters. A forty-item list is Chapter 3's decision paralysis printed out, and its daily non-completion is a shame generator that Chapter 11 cares about. The third rule matters as much as the others: a list that must be remembered to be checked dies by the very failure mode it was built to fix, so it goes on the monitor or the lock screen.

Concept Tested: To-Do Lists That Work

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 4. "Renew the car registration" has sat untouched for three weeks. What breaks the dam?
docs.text:
1. Blocking out two hours on the calendar to handle it properly
  2. Adding it to the top of the list in capital letters
  3. Waiting for the deadline to supply urgency
  4. Naming the physically next thing — "find the renewal notice on the counter and put it by the laptop" — which asks nothing of planning, only of doing
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In the chapter's example the ninety-second version breaks a three-week stall. Most "procrastination" on projects is an undefined next action: the starter motor has nothing its size to grab. The test of a real next action is that you could do it right now without deciding anything further — and if a step still produces the avoidance feeling, split that step again. Option A schedules the same undefined project, which changes nothing about why it stalled.

Concept Tested: Defining Next Actions

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 5. Someone insists getting ready takes eight minutes, is late constantly, and is baffled each time. What changes the departure math?
docs.text:
1. Timing three real mornings and using the revised number, since the feel of duration never updates on its own
  2. Reminding her more firmly that she is always late
  3. Adding a fifteen-minute buffer to every plan without telling her
  4. Accepting the estimate but leaving earlier
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The technique is measure, don't vibe: write the guess before a recurring task, write the actual after, review weekly. Dana's eight-minute belief survives only because it is never confronted with data — three logged mornings reveal twenty-six, and the revised number, not self-scolding, is what changes the math. The chapter adds two rules of thumb while calibration builds: multiply gut estimates for boring multi-step tasks by 1.5 to 2, and schedule backward from hard deadlines.

Concept Tested: Time Estimation

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 6. A wife wants to help her husband get through the taxes. What does body doubling ask of her — and what does it forbid?
docs.text:
1. Work through the forms jointly so the load is shared
  2. Check in every thirty minutes on his progress
  3. Sit nearby with her own book, resisting the urge to narrate, correct, or supervise — supervision converts a body double into a foreman and cancels the effect
  4. Set up the paperwork for him and leave the room entirely
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Body doubling means doing your work in the presence of another person who is simply there — working on their own things, not helping, not supervising. The mechanism maps onto Chapter 2: mild arousal, a whiff of social accountability, and a little interest-currency. Because mere presence is what does the work, options A and B both replace it with something else, and B specifically triggers the foreman failure the chapter warns about.

Concept Tested: Body Doubling

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 7. Two people want to hold each other accountable for weekly admin. Which design does the chapter endorse?
docs.text:
1. A spouse checking in nightly, since proximity aids consistency
  2. A mutual promise to keep each other on track, revisited when needed
  3. Stakes with real consequences, so the commitment carries weight
  4. A specific person expecting a specific thing at a specific time, with friendly stakes, and a peer rather than a spouse
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Accountability works by manufacturing an external deadline — the reward system that ignores "someday" responds to "Casey is standing outside at 7." Option B supplies none of that specificity. Option C misses the hard-won rule that shame-based accountability gets avoided along with the task, so the partner you start dodging becomes a second deadline problem. The peer-not-spouse preference exists because Chapter 14 has strong opinions about what chronic monitor-roles do to a marriage.

Concept Tested: Accountability Partners

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 8. A family sets a new routine to run at 7:15 each morning. It works on weekdays and collapses every weekend. What is the design flaw?
docs.text:
1. Weekends should be exempt from routines entirely
  2. The routine is anchored to a clock time rather than to an existing fixed event — "after the coffee finishes" survives weekends and "at 7:15" doesn't
  3. The routine needs a stronger reward attached to weekend completion
  4. The routine has too few steps to build momentum
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Anchoring to an existing fixed event is the first of the chapter's routine rules, and this is the exact failure it prevents. The other rules matter here too: keep chains to three-to-five steps because long routines fail at their weakest link, externalize the sequence itself on a checklist, and rebuild shrunk after a collapse. Option D inverts the length rule — the two-step version that runs beats the seven-step version that doesn't.

Concept Tested: Routines And Habits

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 9. Someone installs five new habits in one motivated weekend. What does the chapter predict, and what should they do instead?
docs.text:
1. It will hold if the habits are all attached to the same anchor
  2. It will hold, since motivation is the limiting factor and it is currently high
  3. It is a Chapter 3 abandoned-hobby story waiting to happen — stack one new link at a time
  4. It will hold provided each habit has its own alarm
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Habit stacking attaches a new habit directly onto an existing automatic one — after I pour the coffee, I take the medication — so the existing habit becomes the cue and the trigger lives in the environment's sequence rather than in remembering. But the chapter is explicit that a five-link stack installed in one motivated weekend follows the abandoned-hobby curve. Options B and D treat motivation or alarms as sufficient, when the constraint is how many new links can bed in at once.

Concept Tested: Habit Stacking

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 10. A family spends one Saturday and $40 on a key bowl, a charger shelf, a launchpad table, a whiteboard, and three alarms — and their four most frequent fights stop. What principle does this illustrate?
docs.text:
1. Nobody's brain changed; the house got smarter — willpower stored in furniture
  2. The fights were never really about the forgotten items
  3. Financial investment signals commitment, which drives the behavior change
  4. Household conflict is best resolved by reducing the number of shared responsibilities
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Rosa's family stopped relitigating her forgetting and spent an afternoon on infrastructure instead. Environment design has two rules pointing in opposite directions: add friction to the wrong things (the phone charges in the kitchen during homework) and remove it from the right ones (the gym bag by the door, the vitamins on the coffee maker). Each moved object is a decision pre-made and a temptation pre-blocked. The chapter's summary line is that the four most common fights now have no occasion.

Concept Tested: Environment Design

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: Quiz: Building Daily Systems
docs.text: Test your understanding of externalizing memory, capture systems, and the daily-system toolkit for an ADHD brain with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does "externalizing memory" mean in this chapter?
docs.text:
1. Memorizing information more thoroughly through repetition
  2. Relying entirely on someone else to remember things for you
  3. Moving information out of your head and into reliable external storage — paper, phone, alarms — the moment it arrives
  4. A medical procedure that improves memory function
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Externalizing memory means moving information out of your head into reliable external storage the instant it arrives, patching working memory's leaks and prospective memory's unreliable alarm. Option A describes the opposite approach, relying more on internal memory. Option B misplaces the responsibility onto another person rather than an external system. Option D confuses a practical technique with a medical intervention.

Concept Tested: Externalizing Memory

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 2. What is body doubling?
docs.text:
1. Doing your work in the presence of another person who is simply there, without them helping or supervising
  2. Assigning two people to complete the same task independently for comparison
  3. A therapy technique where a therapist mimics the client's behavior
  4. Scheduling two accountability partners instead of one
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Body doubling means working in the presence of another person who is simply there doing their own thing, supplying mild arousal and social presence without supervision or help. Option B describes parallel task assignment, not shared presence. Option C invents an unrelated clinical technique. Option D confuses body doubling with the separate concept of accountability partners.

Concept Tested: Body Doubling

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 3. What is the Pomodoro technique, as described in this chapter?
docs.text:
1. A method of preparing meals in advance to save time
  2. A type of alarm that only rings once per day
  3. A technique for permanently eliminating the need for breaks
  4. Committing to one task for a fixed sprint (classically 25 minutes), followed by a short timed break, repeated
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Pomodoro technique packages timers into a work rhythm: a fixed sprint, classically 25 minutes, followed by a short timed break, repeated with longer breaks every few cycles. Option A is an unrelated meal-planning concept. Option B misdescribes it as a single alarm rather than a repeating rhythm. Option C is the opposite of the technique, which deliberately builds in sanctioned breaks.

Concept Tested: Pomodoro Technique

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 4. Why does the chapter say alarms and timers should be labeled with their action (such as "PHARMACY before home") rather than left blank?
docs.text:
1. Labels are not actually necessary; any alarm works the same way
  2. Labels are required by phone manufacturers
  3. An unlabeled alarm firing later becomes a mystery rather than an instruction, since the intention behind it was never externalized in a retrievable form
  4. Labeled alarms play a different sound than unlabeled ones
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter stresses that an unlabeled alarm going off later is a mystery, not an instruction — labeling the alarm with its action is what makes externalization actually work at the moment it's needed. Option A contradicts the chapter's explicit advice. Option B invents an unrelated technical requirement. Option D is a fabricated claim about alarm sounds.

Concept Tested: Timers And Alarms

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 5. Why does this chapter recommend anchoring routines to an existing fixed event (like "after the coffee finishes") rather than a specific clock time (like "at 7:15")?
docs.text:
1. An event-anchored cue survives schedule disruptions like weekends, while a clock-time cue is more fragile and easily missed
  2. Clock times are technically impossible to use for routines
  3. Anchoring to events is required by law in some states
  4. Clock times work better for people with ADHD than event anchors do
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter explains that "after the coffee finishes" survives weekends and schedule changes, while "at 7:15" is a more fragile cue that's easy to miss when the day's rhythm shifts. Option B is factually false; clock times can be used, just less reliably for this purpose. Option C is an invented and irrelevant claim. Option D reverses the chapter's actual recommendation.

Concept Tested: Routines And Habits

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 6. Why does defining a concrete "next action" (like "find the renewal notice and put it by the laptop") often break through weeks of stalled procrastination, according to this chapter?
docs.text:
1. Because it makes the task more important than it was before
  2. Because most stalled procrastination is actually an undefined next action — the starter motor has nothing sized correctly to grab, and a small, concrete, decision-free step gives it something to start
  3. Because writing anything down guarantees task completion
  4. Because next actions eliminate the need to ever finish the larger project
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter argues that most procrastination on projects is an undefined next action problem — the starter motor needs something specific and small enough to grab, illustrated by the ninety-second registration renewal example. Option A misattributes the mechanism to perceived importance. Option C overstates what mere writing accomplishes without concreteness. Option D confuses a starting step with skipping the rest of the project.

Concept Tested: Defining Next Actions

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 7. A parent wants to help their teenager start using a planner. Based on this chapter's guidance, which approach fits best?
docs.text:
1. Buy an elaborate planner as a surprise gift and expect the teen to adopt it immediately
  2. Set up every feature of the planner in one sitting to save time later
  3. Require the teen to use the planner exactly as designed with no adjustments allowed
  4. Build the system together with the teen's input, starting with one small piece like a daily three-item list, rather than imposing a complete system all at once
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter's closing diagnosis of a failed planner gift stresses that systems built with the person, starting small and added to gradually, succeed where imposed, all-at-once systems collapse. Option A describes exactly the imposed-gift pattern the chapter diagnoses as a common failure. Option B risks the "installed everything at once" collapse the chapter warns about. Option C removes the tinkering and iteration the chapter treats as essential.

Concept Tested: Habit Stacking

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 8. A person wants to stop reaching for their phone during homework time. Which environment design move from this chapter best fits this goal?
docs.text:
1. Leave the phone on the desk but ask themselves to resist checking it through willpower alone
  2. Charge the phone in the kitchen during homework time, so distraction requires extra physical effort to reach
  3. Delete all apps from the phone permanently
  4. Set a phone alarm reminding them not to check the phone
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's environment design principle is to add friction to the wrong things — charging the phone in the kitchen during homework is exactly the kind of friction-adding move it recommends. Option A relies on willpower, which the chapter explicitly argues systems should replace. Option C is a far more drastic step than the chapter suggests. Option D uses the phone itself as the reminder, undermining the whole point of removing it from reach.

Concept Tested: Environment Design

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 9. Someone has a today-list with forty items and feels paralyzed every morning looking at it. Based on this chapter, what is the recommended fix?
docs.text:
1. Add even more items to make sure nothing is forgotten
  2. Memorize the forty items instead of writing them down
  3. Keep a separate everything-list, but limit today's actual list to three-to-five items, physically separated from the larger list
  4. Complete all forty items in a single day through sheer effort
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's rule for to-do lists that work is keeping today's list to three-to-five items, physically separate from the everything-list, since a forty-item list produces decision paralysis and daily non-completion shame. Option A worsens the exact problem described. Option B contradicts the externalization principle underlying the whole chapter. Option D is an unrealistic demand the chapter never recommends.

Concept Tested: To-Do Lists That Work

See: Chapter 9

docs.title: 10. A person, newly excited about this chapter, installs a capture app, a new to-do list system, an estimation log, a Pomodoro timer, a body-doubling schedule, and a full morning and evening routine all in the same weekend. By Thursday, none of it is being used. Using this chapter's analysis, what best explains the collapse?
docs.text:
1. Installing many new systems at once collides with the novelty curve and habit fragility this chapter describes; the fix is one system at a time, rebuilt smaller after any collapse, not abandoned as a character failure
  2. The person simply lacks the willpower required to maintain systems
  3. None of these systems actually work for anyone with ADHD
  4. The collapse proves the person doesn't actually want to improve
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter names this exact pattern as the classic failure mode: installing every system in one inspired weekend collides with the novelty curve and the fragility of new habits, and the fix is starting with one system at a time and rebuilding smaller after a collapse. Option B revives the willpower myth the book has already retired. Option C overgeneralizes from a design mistake to blanket ineffectiveness. Option D wrongly reads a predictable systems failure as a statement about motivation or desire.

Concept Tested: Routines And Habits

See: Chapter 9
