docs.title: The Accommodations Pathway Navigator
docs.text:
Run The Accommodations Pathway Navigator Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/accommodations-pathway-navigator/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Families fail accommodation processes at specific steps — the verbal request that started no clocks, the plan that was never reviewed, the letters never activated. This navigator maps both US pathways from Chapter 12: K-12 (written request → school evaluation → the 504-versus-IEP fork → maintenance) and college (student self-identifies → documentation → interactive process → per-term activation). Every node opens with what happens there, what goes in writing, and the classic mistake.

Load a scenario — Amara (the 504 path her mother's written request unlocked), Dev (the IEP path his dyslexia required), or the college freshman — and the path lights up. The who-owns-each-step toggle color-codes ownership, making the chapter's hardest lesson visual: every node on the college path is student-green, and there is no parent slot in it.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Walk both paths (5 min): Click every node on each side; collect the classic mistakes.
  2. Fork logic (3 min): At the decision diamond, discuss which of your real cases fits 504 versus IEP.
  3. Handoff (3 min): Toggle ownership. Parents list which orange/purple steps they currently perform for a student within three years of the college path.
  4. Paper trail (2 min): List the documents a complete path generates — request email, report, plan, letters.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 12: School And College — both pathways in full
  • Chapter 5: Getting A Diagnosis — the evaluation report both paths reuse

docs.title: The Adult Diagnosis Journey Map
docs.text:
Run the Adult Diagnosis Journey Map Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/adult-diagnosis-journey-map/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The late-diagnosis journey of Chapter 4 has a recognizable arc, and people mid-journey are steadied by knowing where they are on it. This map draws the seven stations — trigger, recognition, deciding to seek help, the gauntlet, the evaluation, the result, and the aftermath — along a winding path. Click any station for its content, including the near-universal "what if I'm faking?" doubt (named and normalized) and the relief-braided-with-grief double bind at the end.

The emotion strip shows the typical feeling at each station. The family view toggle re-annotates every station for the book's second reader: what a supporter can usefully do at that stage — and the well-meant moves that backfire, from the eleven forwarded articles to "at least you know now" in month one.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Locate (2 min): If someone in the room is on this journey, ask them (privately or aloud) to find their station.
  2. Walk (5 min): Click through all seven in order, reading the person-view content.
  3. Switch roles (5 min): Toggle family view and re-walk. Family members note which "not useful" item they've already done — most find at least one; that's normal too.
  4. Debrief (2 min): Discuss the aftermath station's rule: relief and grief coexist and neither cancels.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 4: ADHD Across The Lifespan — the adult diagnosis journey
  • Chapter 5: Getting A Diagnosis — what happens inside station five

docs.title: Attention Spotlight Simulator
docs.text:
Run the Attention Spotlight Simulator Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/attention-spotlight-simulator/main.html" height="482px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This MicroSim puts you in the operator's seat of the attention spotlight from Chapter 1. Your mouse steers the beam. The task is simple and boring on purpose: keep the beam on the green-ringed target ("The form") for sixty seconds while distractors — the phone, the TV, chatter — pulse and try to grab it. When a pulsing distractor captures the beam, it sticks for two seconds before you can pull away, and a caption names what happened.

The controls model the chapter's vocabulary directly:

  • Time on target measures sustaining attention
  • Captures measure resisting capture
  • Task switch mode moves the target every fifteen seconds and measures your shift cost
  • The Distraction slider raises the environment's load — same task, same effort, harder steering

Raising the distraction level models what a higher-ADHD-load environment feels like: the task never changed, but holding it got harder.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min): Before running, have learners guess their time-on-target percentage at distraction level 5.
  2. Run (2 min): One 60-second session at level 5. Compare the result to the prediction.
  3. Manipulate (3 min): Repeat at distraction 0 and distraction 10. Discuss: what changed — the person, or the environment?
  4. Extend (3 min): Turn on task switch mode. Discuss why the moments after each switch feel expensive, and connect to transition struggles at home.
  5. Debrief (2 min): Map each on-screen number to the chapter's skill names: sustaining, resisting capture, shifting.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What ADHD Is And Is Not — the attention skills this simulation demonstrates
  • p5.js Reference

docs.title: Brain Construction Schedule Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Brain Construction Schedule Explorer Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/brain-construction-explorer/main.html" height="482px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The brain is a construction project that runs into the mid-twenties, in a strict back-to-front order — and the self-management (prefrontal) region is installed last. This explorer makes the schedule visible: drag the age slider (or press Play) and watch five regions fill with color as they mature. Click any region to learn what it handles and when it typically comes online.

Below the head, a life demands track lights up kindergarten, homework, driving, and college as the slider passes them — demands that arrive on a fixed schedule regardless of the panel's wiring. Turn on the ADHD trajectory toggle and only the prefrontal region shifts two-to-three years later, making Chapter 2's house-built-while-you-live-in-it example explorable. Fills are illustrative of the maturation ordering, not clinical measurements.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Play (2 min): Run the animation from 0 to 30 once. Ask: which region finished first, which last?
  2. Probe (3 min): Click each region at age 8. Note that emotion runs near full strength while self-management is half-built — discuss what that predicts about tantrums.
  3. Compare (4 min): Set age to 16 (driver's license). Read the prefrontal percentage with the ADHD toggle off, then on. Discuss the caption under the demands track.
  4. Connect (2 min): Relate to the maturation-lag section of Chapter 2 and the "expecting hardware that isn't installed yet" idea.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 2: The ADHD Brain — brain development and the maturation lag
  • Brain Development Timeline — the same finding as a two-curve graph

docs.title: Brain Development Timeline
docs.text:
Run the Brain Development Timeline Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/brain-development-timeline/main.html" height="482px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Brain-imaging research found that in ADHD, the brain's self-management (prefrontal) regions develop along the normal trajectory — roughly two to three years later. This MicroSim makes that finding explorable. Two curves show percent-developed from age 4 to 25: gray for typical development, orange for the ADHD trajectory. Drag the age slider and the infobox reads out both values plus the gap in plain terms: "At age 8, ADHD: about what a typical 5-6 year old has."

The demand line checkbox overlays what the environment expects at each age (sit still at 5, homework alone at 10, run your own schedule at 18). The shaded area where demands exceed the orange curve is the struggle zone — and the three clickable markers (school entry, middle school, college) explain why crises cluster at those ages.

The curves are illustrative of the published trajectory shape, not clinical measurements of any individual.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Read (3 min): Set the cursor to the age of a child you know. Read all three numbers aloud.
  2. Interpret (3 min): Discuss the sentence "expecting age-typical self-control is billing for hardware that isn't installed yet."
  3. Overlay (4 min): Turn on the demand line. Click each milestone marker. Ask: where is the struggle zone widest, and what does that predict?
  4. Extend (2 min): Note where the curves converge. Discuss what remains different in adulthood and why ADHD is a lifespan condition.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What ADHD Is And Is Not — the delayed-maturation finding
  • Chapter 2: The ADHD Brain — prefrontal development and the maturation lag
  • Shaw et al., PNAS 2007 — the longitudinal cortical-thickness study behind the trajectory shape

docs.title: The Capstone Builder
docs.text:
Run The Capstone Builder Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/capstone-builder/main.html" height="622px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The book ends with homework: Chapter 15's two capstone documents, written by each reader for the other. This builder walks you through them section by section. Choose your role — I have ADHD (the eight-section Personal Owner's Manual) or I'm the family (the six-section Family Support Plan) — and each section presents a prompt card: its purpose, two or three starter questions, an example line from the book's running characters, and the chapters it draws on. The blank-page barrier gets the Chapter 12 treatment; the words remain entirely yours.

Drafts save automatically to your browser's local storage — nothing leaves your device. Assemble produces the full document with a date stamp, review date line, and — honestly — any sections still empty, marked rather than hidden. Print it, then follow the exchange instructions: a real date, dinner attached, read all of it before responding, and the masking and our-lines sections get read twice.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Draft (15+ min, often across days): Each reader completes their document. Out of order is fine; the rail tracks progress.
  2. Assemble and print (2 min): Empty sections stay visible — they're the honest to-do list.
  3. Exchange (the point): A scheduled dinner. Two questions before any edit.
  4. Calendar (1 min): The annual review date goes on the shared calendar before the table is cleared.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 15: Partners And Caring For The Caregiver — both capstone templates
  • Chapter 14: Family Life And Communication — the agreements and lines the Support Plan writes down

docs.title: The ADHD Comorbidity Map
docs.text:
Run The ADHD Comorbidity Map Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/comorbidity-map/main.html" height="560px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 6 explains that co-occurring conditions crowd around ADHD through three mechanisms — shared biological roots, consequences of the unexplained years, and mutual entanglement — plus a fourth relationship that is really about differential diagnosis (the look-alikes). This map encodes each mechanism as an edge type. Click any condition for its field-guide entry: definition, relationship, the tell that should prompt screening, and its treatment lane.

The filter buttons isolate one mechanism class at a time — filtering to consequences shows what the untreated years manufacture; filtering to entangled shows what must be treated in parallel. The Dev, 15 button loads the chapter's case: ADHD plus a reading disability plus emerging low mood, with the daily-defeat edge drawn in — the picture that explains why "raise the dose" was the wrong dial.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Tour (4 min): Click through all twelve conditions; note each tell.
  2. Mechanisms (4 min): Use the filters. Ask: which class responds to treating the ADHD itself, and which needs its own lane?
  3. Case (3 min): Load Dev. Trace why the stimulant dial couldn't fix 10th grade.
  4. Screen (3 min): Each learner privately marks any tell that rings true — that list is the agenda for the next clinician visit.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 6: Co-occurring Conditions — the field guide this map renders
  • vis-network documentation

docs.title: The Conflict Cycle Breaker
docs.text:
Run The Conflict Cycle Breaker Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/conflict-cycle-breaker/main.html" height="522px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 14's conflict loop, drawn as a ring you can operate: demand at a bad moment → disappointing response → escalated repetition → RSD spike → blowup → ledgers updated → ambient tension rises → and back around, faster each turn. Click any stage for its anatomy, sample dialogue, and — color-coded on the border — who can act there.

The green exits are the chapter's argument that either person can cut the loop at any point: time the demand and system carries the reminder belong to the family member; the pause belongs to the person with ADHD; repair and call the loop belong to either. Each exit shows its replacement sentence — "want me to add it to the board?" instead of "did you do it YET?" — and cutting an edge is sticky: press Run one turn afterward and watch the turn stop dead at your cut. That's analysis turned into rehearsal.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Watch it spin (2 min): Run one turn untouched, reading the dialogue.
  2. Anatomy (4 min): Click all seven stages. Each family identifies the stage their loop usually ignites at.
  3. Cut it (4 min): Each person cuts the exit they own, reads the replacement sentence aloud, and re-runs the turn.
  4. Agree (3 min): Pick one replacement sentence to actually adopt this week, and put its supporting system (the board, the pause protocol) in place.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 14: Family Life And Communication — the loop and its exits
  • Chapter 11: Emotional Life And Identity — the RSD spike and the pause
  • The Stigma Cycle — the same loop structure at cultural scale

docs.title: The Disclosure Decision Navigator
docs.text:
Run The Disclosure Decision Navigator Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/disclosure-decision-navigator/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 13 frames workplace disclosure as a strategic decision with real trade-offs — not a moral test of self-acceptance. This navigator renders the graduated ladder: the informal specific ask (no diagnosis attached, nothing to un-ring), partial disclosure ("a medical condition that affects attention"), and formal ADA disclosure (in writing, through HR, with the timing rule: before a performance crisis, never after). Click any level for its sample script, what it gets, what it risks, and when to escalate.

Set the five factor chips — workplace size, manager relationship, performance situation, stigma climate, need for legal protection — and the ladder highlights where your factors favor starting, always as decision support rather than a verdict. Four scenarios (including the bad-review-season timing case) come pre-set with reasoning. The principle bar stays fixed: deciding not to disclose is also a legitimate outcome.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Ladder (4 min): Read all three levels' scripts aloud. Note what each can't be (undone).
  2. Scenarios (4 min): Run all four; before reading the reasoning, predict the favored level.
  3. Your factors (3 min): Set the chips for a real situation. Discuss with the trusted sounding board — then respect whatever the person decides.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 13: Work And Career — the ADA, accommodations, and the disclosure decision
  • Chapter 11: Emotional Life And Identity — the mechanism-pattern-ask formula the scripts use

docs.title: Distraction Defense Lab
docs.text:
Run the Distraction Defense Lab Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/distraction-defense-lab/main.html" height="482px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 10 makes an architectural claim: single distraction defenses fail independently, and stacks degrade gracefully. This lab lets you test it on your own runs. Toggle four defenses — physical distance, unblock friction, notification silence, and a visible sprint timer — and run a simulated hour. Capture events break the green focus bar with labels ("notification → video spiral"), shields mark attempts a defense caught, and the readout reports focused minutes, captures, the longest unbroken stretch, and the re-entry toll.

Run the honest baseline first (no defenses — usually under 25 focused minutes of 60). Then compare single defenses against the full stack in the comparison strip. The bad day toggle weakens every defense 30% — demonstrating why stacks matter most exactly when resolve is lowest.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Baseline (2 min): Zero defenses. Read the honest number.
  2. Single layers (4 min): One run per single defense. Note what each couldn't stop.
  3. Stack (3 min): All four. Compare the strip. Note that even the stack lets one small capture through — defenses reduce, never eliminate.
  4. Bad day (2 min): Re-run the stack with bad day on. Discuss why architecture beats willpower on exactly those days.
  5. Install (2 min): Each learner names the one layer missing from their real setup.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 10: Tools And Keeping Systems Alive — the defense stack
  • Chapter 3: Presentations And Everyday Traits — the re-entry toll

docs.title: The Ninety-Second Storm Explorer
docs.text:
Run The Ninety-Second Storm Explorer Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/emotion-storm-explorer/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 11's core regulation fact: the surge peaks and begins to fall within roughly ninety seconds if it isn't refueled by action. This explorer makes that steerable. A trigger lands — the "ok" text, the boss's summons, the unpaid-bill conversation — and the surge spikes RSD-fast. At three decision points you choose: a pause move (draft-don't-send, "I'm taking ten," the physical dump), a reframe (pick a plausible alternative reading and hold two hypotheses), or acting on it now — which visibly refuels the curve.

Each scenario ends by revealing what was actually true. Deliberately, some alarms are real — the skills' value never depended on the alarm being false: entering a real problem at intensity 30 beats entering it at 95. The family view toggle annotates each decision point with what a bystander does that helps (reassure) versus escalates (litigate the trigger's size). The score that matters: time above intensity 70.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Feel the physics (3 min): Run one scenario choosing "Act on it NOW" every time. Watch the curve never land.
  2. Steer (4 min): Replay with pause moves and reframes. Compare time-above-70.
  3. Mixed truth (3 min): Run the unpaid-bill scenario. Discuss why the skills still paid off when the concern was real.
  4. Family view (3 min): Re-run with the toggle on. Family members practice the reassure line out loud.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 11: Emotional Life And Identity — emotion regulation skills and RSD
  • Chapter 14: Family Life And Communication — the pause protocol and repair

docs.title: Anatomy of a Thorough Evaluation
docs.text:
Run the Anatomy of a Thorough Evaluation Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/evaluation-anatomy-map/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 5 teaches that any legitimate ADHD evaluation is built from the same components. This map lays them out around the diagnostic conclusion: the clinical interview (the spine), rating scales, self-report, collateral information, childhood history, and — drawn dashed because they're optional or single data points — neuropsych testing and computer attention tests. Two diamond gates carry the criteria: onset before 12, and real impairment in two or more settings (with its known blind spot: high-achievement masking). Click anything for what it contributes, its limits, and the red flag of its absence.

Rate-this-evaluation mode is the payoff: four vignette evaluations — from the 20-minute prescription mill to the solid two-session workup — that you judge thorough or insufficient, with feedback naming the exact components present or missing. That judgment is the consumer skill the chapter exists to build.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Tour (4 min): Click all seven components and both gates. Note which two are dashed and why.
  2. Rate (5 min): Judge all four vignettes. Discuss the telehealth one — what makes it insufficient isn't the video call.
  3. Apply (3 min): Draft the two questions you'd ask a prospective evaluator, using the map as the checklist.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 5: Getting A Diagnosis — the evaluation anatomy
  • Chapter 4: ADHD Across The Lifespan — why the impairment gate misses maskers

docs.title: Executive Function Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Executive Function Explorer Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/executive-function-explorer/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 2 argues that "she knows how to do this" was never the point — executive functions are the skills that manage other skills, and they fail one component at a time. This explorer gives each of the six components a card: click to expand it into its definition, concrete examples at three ages, the judgment that failure usually attracts ("lazy," "rude," "careless"), and the replacement question a family should ask instead.

Quiz mode is the point of the exercise: an everyday scenario appears ("he agreed to take out the trash, walked past it four times, and swears he still meant to") and you attribute it to the right component. The feedback explains the attribution — and why the near-misses differ. That attribution move is exactly what the chapter wants families doing at home instead of reaching for character verdicts.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 min): Open all six cards. Each learner names the component that hits hardest in their own household.
  2. Quiz (5 min): Run all ten scenarios. Note which attributions were hardest.
  3. Apply (5 min): Each learner writes one real scenario from their week and the group attributes it using the cards.
  4. Debrief (2 min): Compare the "judged as" line with the "ask instead" line for the component your household picked.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 2: The ADHD Brain — the six components and their table
  • Chapter 14: Family Life And Communication — talking to the mechanism, not the character

  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts. Use "Check All" or "Uncheck All" for bulk operations.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

docs.title: Lifespan Demands and Scaffolding Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Lifespan Demands and Scaffolding Explorer Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/lifespan-scaffolding-explorer/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 4's most useful pattern in one picture: across seven life stages, executive demands rise while external scaffolding drops — and the shaded gap between the lines is what a person must supply themselves. Click any stage name for its typical ADHD picture, what scaffolding just dropped, and the classic failure mode. The college cliff is unmistakable: demands near their maximum exactly where scaffolding hits its minimum.

Two controls carry the chapter's argument. The rebuild toggle overlays a third line — support deliberately rebuilt through planners, coaching, accommodations, and family agreements — visibly narrowing the gap (that line is what Part Three of the book builds). And Follow Amara walks the chapter's undiagnosed case across the stages: coping, coping, straining, collapse at college — then asks where an observer would first notice anything, versus where the condition was present.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Read the shape (3 min): Identify the widest gap before toggling anything. Ask why crises cluster there.
  2. Stage stories (4 min): Click each stage; have learners match a person they know to a stage.
  3. Amara (3 min): Step through the walkthrough. Discuss why "she was fine until college" misreads the data.
  4. Rebuild (3 min): Toggle the third line. Ask which specific supports would move your stage's green dot up.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 4: ADHD Across The Lifespan — transitions and the scaffolding cliff
  • Chapter 12: School And College — transferring systems before the cliff

docs.title: Myth or Evidence Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Myth or Evidence Sorter Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/myth-or-evidence-sorter/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The sorter deals claims about ADHD one at a time — some drawn straight from Chapter 1's myth section, some from the research facts around it. You must commit to a judgment (Myth or Supported by evidence) before the card flips; the reveal always comes with a two-to-three sentence explanation naming the concept the answer rests on — attention regulation, heritability, the DSM-5 counting rules, masking.

A round is ten claims. The summary lists anything you missed, with its explanation, so a replay targets exactly the beliefs that need updating. The prediction-before-reveal design is deliberate: judging first is what makes this an evaluation exercise instead of a reading exercise.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Baseline (5 min): Each learner plays one solo round and notes their score.
  2. Pair round (5 min): Pairs replay, debating each claim aloud before committing. Scores usually rise — discuss why.
  3. Family variant (5 min): The person with ADHD and a family member play together; each privately predicts which claims the other will miss.
  4. Debrief (3 min): Collect the most-missed claims and trace each to its chapter section.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What ADHD Is And Is Not — the myths and the evidence
  • Chapter 5: Getting A Diagnosis — the DSM-5 counting rules several claims test

docs.title: Next-Action Trainer
docs.text:
Run the Next-Action Trainer Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/next-action-trainer/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 9 calls defining next actions the single highest-value habit in the toolkit: most "procrastination" on projects is an undefined next action — the starter motor has nothing its size to grab. This trainer rehearses the skill in two modes.

Judge mode shows a stalled task and four candidates ("work on the application," "think about essay topics," "open the portal and screenshot the requirements list," "be more organized") — pick the real one, and the feedback names the exact test each failure flunks: topic-not-action, requires further decisions, not physically specifiable, character-goal. Build mode hands you a vague project and a text box; forgiving heuristics check for a doing-verb, a specific object, and project-smell, then ask the chain question: and after that? Three links teaches the deepest lesson — you never needed to plan the whole project, only the next ninety seconds.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Judge (4 min): Run all six judge tasks. Tally which failure type each learner picks most.
  2. Build (5 min): Each learner builds a three-link chain for one sim task, then for one real task from their own list.
  3. Install (2 min): The real task's first link goes on tonight's today-list (Chapter 9's three-item rule).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 9: Building Daily Systems — task breakdown and next actions
  • Chapter 10: Tools And Keeping Systems Alive — starting rituals and the five-minute contract

docs.title: Reward Discounting Simulator
docs.text:
Run the Reward Discounting Simulator Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/reward-discounting-simulator/main.html" height="482px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 2 calls the ADHD reward system an economist with a broken discount rate: rewards lose motivational value unusually fast as they move away in time. This simulator draws both discount curves — typical (gray, gentle) and ADHD-steep (orange, collapsing) — from the same reward, with a red motivation threshold line below which tasks simply don't start. Drag the reward marker along the delay axis and the readout shows what each brain feels the reward is worth, and whether it starts or stalls.

The four intervention chips are the chapter's strategy logic made physical: Today-sized piece and Deadline tomorrow move the payoff near now; Body double and Make it a game lift the whole curve by paying in currencies this system accepts. Every chip explains its mechanism when applied. The preset scenarios (the three-week assignment, the gym habit, the registration renewal) each start below threshold — your job is to rescue them.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Observe (2 min): Load "Assignment due in 3 weeks." Read both felt values. Note which brain's value sits below threshold.
  2. Predict (2 min): Before clicking any chip, predict which single intervention rescues it. Test.
  3. Compare (4 min): Rescue each preset scenario with the fewest chips. Discuss why different tasks need different currencies.
  4. Transfer (3 min): Each learner names one stalled real task and the chip they'll apply this week.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 2: The ADHD Brain — delay aversion and the interest-based nervous system
  • Chapter 9: Building Daily Systems — the interventions as daily practice

docs.title: The Stigma Cycle
docs.text:
Run The Stigma Cycle Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/stigma-cycle-diagram/main.html" height="522px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Stigma isn't a single event — it's a feedback loop. This diagram renders the six-stage cycle from Chapter 1 as a ring: public stigma feeds hiding, hiding delays diagnosis, unexplained struggle attracts myth explanations, the myths get internalized as self-stigma, self-stigma worsens the visible struggle, and visible struggle refreshes the public stigma. Click any stage for its concrete example (drawn from the chapter's teacher story) and how it feeds the next stage.

The two green dashed nodes are the break points. Click Accurate information and the struggle-to-myths edge goes gray — a mechanism caption replaces a character verdict. Click Family uses the regulation lens and the myths-to-self-stigma edge cuts — because for one person's daily life, family is the loudest culture there is. In fullscreen mode you can also drag, zoom, and pan.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Trace (3 min): Click each stage in order, reading its example aloud. Ask: where does this loop run in stories you know?
  2. Analyze (3 min): Ask which stages are visible to outsiders and which are private. (Only stages 1 and 6 are public — the loop mostly runs unseen.)
  3. Intervene (4 min): Click each break point. Discuss which one this family or classroom controls, and what the replacement behavior sounds like in an actual sentence.
  4. Extend (2 min): Connect to Chapter 14's conflict cycle — same loop structure, kitchen-table scale.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What ADHD Is And Is Not — the stigma section this diagram renders
  • Chapter 11: Emotional Life And Identity — self-stigma and its repair
  • vis-network documentation

docs.title: Symptom and Presentation Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Symptom and Presentation Explorer Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/symptom-presentation-explorer/main.html" height="482px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Every ADHD evaluation counts the same eighteen behaviors. This explorer puts the actual decision procedure in your hands: toggle symptom chips in the two DSM-5 columns, watch the live counters, and see the resulting presentation the moment a column crosses the threshold — six symptoms for children, five from age seventeen (the Adult checkbox moves the line). Hovering any chip names the executive function underneath it, connecting the checklist back to Chapter 2's machinery.

Three presets tell the chapter's stories: Marcus, 9 trips the visible column; Elena, 15 meets full criteria while disturbing no one; and Devon 9 → 39 (click twice) unchecks the visible motor chips and checks the internal ones — the presentation shift that makes "he sits still now" mean nothing. The banner always carries the caution that counts alone never diagnose: the duration, onset, settings, and impairment gates of Chapter 5 still apply.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Operate (3 min): Build a pattern that yields each of the three presentations.
  2. Presets (4 min): Run Marcus, then Elena. Ask: which one gets an evaluation this year, and why isn't it about severity?
  3. Shift (3 min): Run Devon twice. Discuss what "grew out of it" gets wrong.
  4. Threshold (2 min): With five inattentive chips on, toggle the Adult checkbox. Discuss why the DSM lowers the bar at 17.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 3: Presentations And Everyday Traits — symptom criteria and presentations
  • Chapter 5: Getting A Diagnosis — the gates beyond counting

docs.title: Three Traits Across Three Ages Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Three Traits Explorer Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/three-traits-explorer/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The three trait words behind every ADHD diagnosis — inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity — never look the same at six, sixteen, and thirty-six. This explorer lays the nine combinations out as a grid. Click any cell to see concrete example behaviors, a first-person quote from inside that experience, and the misreading that presentation usually attracts.

The "Who gets noticed?" toggle re-shades the grid by how likely each presentation is to trigger a referral for evaluation. The pale cells — quiet inattention, adult restlessness turned inward — are where ADHD hides, and they explain most of the late-diagnosis stories in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Orient (2 min): Ask learners which single cell matches their mental image of "ADHD." (Most pick Hyperactivity/Child.)
  2. Explore (5 min): Click through all nine cells. Have each learner find the cell that best matches someone they know.
  3. Reveal (3 min): Turn on the "Who gets noticed?" toggle. Ask: which cells are dark, which are pale, and who do the pale cells describe?
  4. Connect (3 min): Discuss why girls and adults are diagnosed late using only the grid's shading as evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: What ADHD Is And Is Not — trait definitions
  • Chapter 4: ADHD Across The Lifespan — the diagnosis gap this grid makes visible

docs.title: Time Blindness Challenge
docs.text:
Run the Time Blindness Challenge Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/time-blindness-challenge/main.html" height="452px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Time blindness is a felt phenomenon, so this MicroSim lets you measure your own felt time. Round 1: click when you believe thirty seconds have passed, while drifting shapes gently distract. Round 2: race through a click-the-numbers task, then estimate how long it took. Round 3: predict how long a repeat will take, then do it. The results panel keeps a running felt-versus-actual ledger with signed errors — most people discover that engaging tasks compress felt time dramatically, which is Chapter 3's 5:52-shower example in miniature.

The visible clock toggle is the fix made experiential: replay round 2 with the clock on and the estimation error collapses. Externalized time beats felt time — the exact principle behind the timers and departure alarms of Chapter 10. This is a demonstration, not a diagnostic test.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Baseline (4 min): All three rounds, no clock. Note each error's direction.
  2. Discuss (3 min): Whose errors were largest during the engaging round? Connect to "five more minutes" that was forty.
  3. Fix (3 min): Replay with the visible clock. Compare errors.
  4. Transfer (2 min): Each learner names one recurring task to run an estimation log on this week (guess, time it, compare).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 3: Presentations And Everyday Traits — time blindness
  • Chapter 9: Building Daily Systems — the estimation log

docs.title: Titration Response Tracker
docs.text:
Run the Titration Response Tracker Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/titration-response-tracker/main.html" height="507px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 7 claims that structured tracking converts anecdotes into titration signals. This tracker proves it on Dev's eight weeks: three target symptoms (homework starts, calm mornings, teacher reports) and a side-effect burden line, charted weekly, with every dose step annotated. Hover any week to read the diary note behind the numbers — including week 3's untouched lunch and week 7's flat-at-dinner overshoot.

Decision mode pauses at weeks 3, 5, and 7 and asks you to make the call: hold, step, engineer around a side effect, or step back. The feedback names the data feature that drives each answer — real target response plus a common side effect reads differently than flatness with no target gain. The exercise is about reading data; every real dose decision belongs to the prescriber, and the sim says so.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Read (3 min): Hover weeks 0-8 in order, reading the diary aloud.
  2. Decide (5 min): Make all three calls before reading feedback. Compare answers in pairs.
  3. Transfer (4 min): Have each family draft their own three target symptoms — concrete, observable, theirs — for a real tracking sheet.
  4. Boundary (1 min): Repeat the rule: the sheet informs the prescriber; it never replaces them.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 7: Medication — titration and tracking
  • Chart.js Documentation

docs.title: Treatment Evidence Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Treatment Evidence Explorer Fullscreen

Place the following line in your website to include this MicroSim in your course:

<iframe src="https://arunbatchu.github.io/adhd/sims/treatment-evidence-explorer/main.html" height="562px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Chapter 8 ranks the treatment landscape by where each option's evidence lives on the pyramid — from testimonials at the floor to meta-analyses at the summit. This chart makes the ranking explorable: bar length is evidence strength, color depth is approximate effect magnitude, hover gives the one-line verdict, and clicking a bar opens the full reasoning. Both scales are deliberately qualitative — false precision is its own kind of misinformation.

The claim tester deals six marketplace claims — the five-star supplement, the clinic's internal neurofeedback data, the honestly boring omega-3 sentence — and asks you to place each on its pyramid floor, with explained feedback. The skill being trained: asking which floor does this claim live on before spending money, hours, or hope.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
1. Read the shape (3 min): Which cheap, strong-evidence rows surprise people? (Sleep and parent training, usually.)
  2. Verdicts (4 min): Click neurofeedback and supplements. Discuss the "better controls, smaller effect" tell.
  3. Test (5 min): Run all six claims. Note that the trustworthy claim sounds the most boring.
  4. Audit (3 min): Each family lists what they currently spend on, and its floor.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 8: Treatment Beyond Medication — the evidence hierarchy and honest verdicts
  • Chart.js Documentation
